lb6157.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 12, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security A critical flaw in Apache HTTP Server's HTTP/2 module, mod_http2, can let a remote attacker run code on the server. Tracked as CVE-2026-119618, it affects versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 and is fixed in version 2.4.71, released yesterday. Only servers with HTTP/2 enabled are affected, according to Red Hat, which ships the server as part of Red Hat Enterprise Linux. An attacker who can reach the server needs no authentication to exploit the flaw and could take full control of the server process, the Linux vendor says. It rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. The vendor's assessment, published yesterday, also says "public research has demonstrated a reliable exploit" against a server in its default configuration with mod_http2 enabled. It does not name or link that research. Security company Wiz said later that day that no exploit was available and that no exploitation in the wild had been reported. HTTP/2 runs only where the Protocols directive turns it on, as the module documentation explains. The directive uses h2 for HTTP/2 over TLS and h2c for HTTP/2 over plain TCP. It can be set for the whole server or for a single virtual host, so admins should check the server-wide setting and every virtual host. Standalone builds of the module, released on GitHub as mod_h2, are affected from version 2.0.8 through 2.0.42. Admins who run the Apache HTTP Server project's own releases should move to version 2.4.71, the fixed release named in its security advisory. That release also fixes a crash in mod_md, rated important, and a one-byte overwrite of stack memory in mod_vhost_alias, rated low. The distributions in the table below ship their own builds of the server, with their own package version numbers. On Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9, for example, the fix ships as mod_http2-2.0.26-7.el9_9.1. Red Hat shipped fixes for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 and 10 yesterday and rates the flaw Important on those releases rather than Critical. Their mod_http2 packages give each HTTP/2 stream its own memory allocator, which makes an attack much harder, according to the vendor's severity assessment. Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 and earlier do not contain the vulnerable code. Platform Status Fixed package Apache HTTP Server project releases Fixed 2.4.71 Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 Fixed (RHSA-2026:98981) mod_http2-2.0.26-7.el9_9.1 Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10 Fixed (RHSA-2026:98978) mod_http2-2.0.29-5.el10_3.1 Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9.4 Update Services for SAP Solutions, and 9.6, 9.8, 10.0 and 10.2 Extended Update Support Fixed (RHSA-2026:98968, RHSA-2026:98954, RHSA-2026:98982, RHSA-2026:98953 and RHSA-2026:98979) See each advisory Red Hat Enterprise Linux 6, 7 and 8 Not affected None needed Red Hat JBoss Core Services and Red Hat Hardened Images Affected, no fix listed None listed Debian unstable (sid) Fixed apache2 2.4.71-1 Debian bookworm, trixie and forky Vulnerable None listed Amazon Linux 2 (Core), Amazon Linux 2023 and Amazon Linux 2027 Preview Pending fix None listed Ubuntu No status page None listed The Debian rows come from Debian's security tracker, and the Amazon row from the Amazon Linux tracker. Ubuntu's CVE tracker had no page for the flaw when The Hacker News checked it today. The Apache HTTP Server advisory offers no workaround. In its vulnerability analysis, Wiz advises admins who cannot update yet to remove h2 and h2c from the Protocols directive, leaving Protocols http/1.1. The standalone mod_h2 project has published no fixed release so far. Its release list on GitHub ends at 2.0.42, the last affected version, and its repository has been read-only since it was archived on June 9. The Protocols change above also applies to servers that use those builds. The flaw was reported on October 26 by Anthropic's OSS Scanner, a free scanning service for open-source projects that uses the company's AI models. Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research reported it last week. An earlier HTTP/2 flaw, CVE-2026-23918, was fixed in version 2.4.67, released on May 4. Servers updated to that release, or to any later one up to 2.4.70, still run a version that the new flaw affects.

1ten3cz.text: ConnectWise has taken the precautionary step of disabling five third-party extensions in partner environments following reports of unauthorized access. In an advisory posted on its site, the company said there is no evidence that the incident involves a compromise of its infrastructure or a vulnerability in the ScreenConnect software. "Our initial assessment suggests the activity may involve a threat actor's abuse of independent third-party extensions installed in partner environments," it said. "We are continuing to validate this assessment. The initial access method and full scope remain under investigation." ConnectWise has identified about 400 partner environments with at least one of the third-party extensions installed. It also emphasized that the presence of the extensions alone does not indicate or establish compromise. While these extensions provide an API capable of executing remote commands, access to that API is secured by a passphrase configured by the partner during setup, it added. The list of extensions identified for precautionary disabling is below - Labtech Plus RMM Plus RMM+ RMM Plus Password Link RMM+ Password Link ConnectWise also said it has urged on-premises partners to disable the extensions, and is recommending all partners to ensure security controls are running, preserve suspicious activity logs, and stay vigilant for - Unusual sign-ins, unfamiliar locations, repeated login failures, and unexpected multi-factor authentication (MFA) prompts New administrator accounts or changes to user permissions Unexpected extension installations, remote commands, and Toolbox activity Unapproved remote-access software on customer devices and technician workstations Unexpected support requests, password-reset messages, and software downloads through a trusted channel The company has shared the following indicators of compromise (IoCs) - IP addresses: 185.99.255[.]28 155.94.150[.]39 Domains and URLs: ns[.]mo7sen[.]dev ns[.]mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4 sc[.]payproofkit[.]com cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com newnewnew[.]gotdns[.]org Soxnewwork[.]homedns[.]org Artifacts: sckit-run.bat sckit-decoder.ps1 TrapWatch.ps1 Panel-Lateral.ps1 Run-Lateral-Full.bat runnew.cmd ToolboxRelayUploader.exe Sqlite3.exe Cybersecurity company Huntress, which is also tracking the activity, said it has observed attackers using access to cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to push Run commands with an aim to install rogue ScreenConnect clients on at least 288 managed endpoints across 48 organizations. The activity was first detected on November 11, 2026, at around 5:47 p.m. UTC. Huntress told The Hacker News that it has not seen evidence of a new vulnerability, but noted the exact method through which the attacker got panel access remains unclear. Current telemetry points to compromised credentials or hijacked operator sessions to gain initial access, it said. The overall attack unfolds in a worm-like fashion using a two-step process - Initial access: Attackers use a compromised ScreenConnect panel's Run Command feature to deploy a rogue ScreenClient client across endpoints, creating a persistent backdoor that no longer depends on the original panel. Lateral movement: When a technician connects to an infected endpoint through ScreenConnect, the malware can spread back to their workstation, steal saved browser sessions and authentication tokens, and pivot to other ScreenConnect panels the technician has access to. "The rogue clients deliver SCKit, a custom malicious toolkit that establishes persistent remote access and creates a relay trap for intercepting session cookies," Huntress researchers Ben Nahorney and Susannah Matt said. "The infection path works in two stages: from an infected endpoint to a technician who connects to it, and from a technician's workstation to every endpoint their panel can connect to. However, not all functionality has been observed during observed incidents; some functionality has been discovered through analysing the payloads." SCKit is delivered as an encrypted payload and via a Base64-encoded dropper ("sckit-run.bat"), which then contacts a remote server to fetch a PowerShell payload ("sckit-decoder.ps1") that's responsible for launching the toolkit. Other components of the malware are designed to add Microsoft Defender exclusions, install a second attacker-controlled ScreenConnect client, create a scheduled task named "TrapWatch," and replace the legitimate ScreenConnect installation with an attacker-controlled copy. There are signs that at least one of the scripts is generated by a large language model (LLM) based on the detailed source code references and comments that explain its functionality. "Going beyond what we've observed, we've reconstructed an additional functionality intended to spread from a technician's workstation to the ScreenConnect panel," Huntress said. "This has been discovered from analysis of its scripts, configuration, and tools. To date we have not observed a successful jump from an infected endpoint to a technician workstation, or from that workstation to other endpoints." This involves abusing the connection to fetch a dropper ("Run-Lateral-Full.bat"), which then connects to an external server ("ns.mo7sen[.]dev") to download a loader that gathers the workstation's unique ID, sends it back to the attacker, and returns a tailored encrypted kit for that specific workstation - "Panel-Lateral.ps1," which in conjunction with "LabConfig.ps1," steals the .aspxauth session cookie from the workstation and attempts to replay the cookie against the panel and get the tokens necessary to enumerate any other sessions the technician can access. "ToolboxRelayUploader.exe," which leverages access gained to any other sessions to upload a payload, "WithUninstall.ps1," to the panel's Shared Toolbox. "A panel request tells every reachable session to run the toolbox item," Huntress said. "This payload is designed to run as SYSTEM on those endpoints, installing the trap and extending the cycle. Roughly 60 seconds after the broadcast, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe deletes the Shared Toolbox item." To add to the concern, the threat actor has been observed tagging each compromised managed service provider (MSP) with a sequential number. Huntress said the tags it has observed start partway through the sequence, indicating other MSPs may have been compromised earlier. ScreenConnect users are advised to check their Run Command history even if they haven't received alerts. In a separate alert, Sophos said it has also observed unauthorized ScreenConnect client deployments following the same modus operandi. The activity has originated from three ScreenConnect instance IDs - d905b2b1b165d0a9 4b8f4089ddaac6a9 df1f7ef0cfacd0d8 It's suspected that these are compromised instances that are being used to execute commands and deploy additional malicious instances, whose IDs are below - 2588ef5c15954b10 ed630cc2c873b091 "Curl.exe downloaded ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi from 185.99.255[.]28 to C:\Windows\TEMP\sc.msi," Sophos explained. "A ScreenConnect-generated command file then launched msiexec.exe to install the client silently. The researchers also observed ScreenConnect scripts staging batch files and using PowerShell with execution-policy bypass to retrieve a second-stage script from ns[.]mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4." (This is a developing story. Please check back for more details.)

an6e8t.text: The Baker Tilly Advisory Group is notifying clients that a data breach has compromised certain personal information about them and their dependents. The company said the exposed data was stored on a platform operated by a third-party service provider Baker Tilly uses to serve clients. Baker Tilly learned of the incident on September 6 and completed its review of the affected data on October 28, when it identified whose information was involved. “On September 6, 2026, Baker Tilly became aware of a potential cybersecurity incident involving certain information stored on a platform operated by a third-party service provider used by Baker Tilly in connection with services we provide to clients,” reads the notification to customers. “The unauthorized actor was able to obtain data relating to certain Baker Tilly clients,” the company added. The breach notification does not provide a count of impacted clients, does not name the service provider, and leaves the specific data types exposed as a placeholder. Data from the Office of the Texas Attorney General reports that Baker Tilly impacted 10,456 individuals in the state of Texas alone. The portal lists Social Security numbers (SSNs), full names, addresses, and other information as exposed data types. Baker Tilly is a major accounting firm in the U.S., providing auditing, tax planning, compliance, advisory, and business operations services. Globally, the company operates in 147 countries and reports an annual revenue of $6.8 billion. After discovering the incident, the company says it took immediate steps to contain it, contracted external experts to investigate, and notified law enforcement authorities. Furthermore, it says it currently has no evidence of unauthorized activity on its own network, and added that it has no reports of identity theft or fraud linked to the exposure of customer information. To mitigate the risks arising from the incident, the firm offers affected individuals 24 months of credit and identity monitoring through Experian. BleepingComputer has contacted Baker Tilly for more information about the data breach, its source, the number of affected customers, and the type of data compromised, but we have not received a reply by the time of publishing. 1pryxd1.text: ConnectWise is investigating an active malware campaign targeting managed service providers (MSPs) that uses compromised ScreenConnect environments to deploy rogue remote-access clients to customer devices. The campaign was first discovered Wednesday by cybersecurity firm Huntress, which says it has identified six compromised MSPs and 286 affected endpoints across 47 organizations, and that the number of victims continues to rise. "Our SOC is working an active campaign that started around 17:47 UTC today targeting cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances," Huntress posted to Reddit. "We are currently tracking 6 compromised MSPs and 286+ endpoints, and those numbers are climbing. ConnectWise is engaged and working this with us." ScreenConnect is a remote access and support platform used by MSPs and IT teams to remotely manage and troubleshoot customer devices. According to Huntress, attackers are using ScreenConnect's Run Command functionality to deploy ScreenConnect clients on managed endpoints, providing remote access outside of the legitimate MSP's ScreenConnect environment. The researchers also warned of a potentially more dangerous technique in which attackers can compromise an MSP technician's workstation when they initiate a ScreenConnect session with an infected customer device. It is unclear how this reported reverse-pivot technique works, including whether it exploits a software vulnerability or abuses legitimate ScreenConnect functionality. In a statement to BleepingComputer, ConnectWise confirmed it is investigating the attacks and urged partners to avoid interactive remote sessions with potentially compromised devices. "We are aware of reports of malicious activity affecting a limited number of ScreenConnect partners and are actively investigating," ConnectWise told BleepingComputer. "As a precaution, partners should avoid opening interactive ScreenConnect sessions to suspected compromised devices and use separate security tooling to investigate. Partners should also review account activity, revoke active sessions, reset credentials from a trusted device, and verify multifactor authentication." The company said it would provide further information and guidance through the ConnectWise Trust Center. Huntress has not yet determined how the attackers are gaining access to affected MSP environments, but says their current telemetry points to compromised credentials and hijacked MSP support sessions. Huntress also warned that sequential identifiers used by the attackers suggest additional MSPs may have been previously compromised. “Sequential attacker-assigned tags suggest other MSPs may have been compromised earlier, so ScreenConnect users should check their Run Command history even if they haven’t received alerts,” Huntress told BleepingComputer. Huntress also shared indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help organizations identify malicious activity, including rogue ScreenConnect client IDs and infrastructure used by the attackers. The indicators include: Attacker relay: 185.99.255[.]28 (hostname: screen) C2 domains: newnewnew.gotdns[.]org, soxnewwork.homedns[.]org Possible additional C2: cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com Secondary C2: sc.payproofkit[.]com (155.94.150[.]39, hostname: WIN-FB5CKHMU4E1) Stager: hxxps://ns.mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4 Rogue ScreenConnect client IDs: 2588ef5c15954b10, ed630cc2c873b091 Installer pattern: /Bin/ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi?...&c=Exploited<N> Attacker name: Addmin Files: Panel-Lateral.ps1, runnew.cmd, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe, Run-Lateral-Full.bat The researchers are urging MSPs to review their environments for signs of compromise and avoid initiating interactive ScreenConnect sessions with potentially infected endpoints. BleepingComputer reached out to Huntress with additional questions about the attacks and will update the post if we receive a response. Earlier malware activity linked to rogue ScreenConnect identifier BleepingComputer found an earlier malicious batch script that references one of the rogue ScreenConnect client IDs listed by Huntress, suggesting that the ID was used in malicious activity months before the current attacks were disclosed. The script, named SSA-2026-STATEMENT-15518787.bat [VirusTotal], appears to impersonate a Social Security Administration statement and was first uploaded to VirusTotal on July 25, 2026. The batch file attempts to add Microsoft Defender exclusions and creates persistence through the Windows Startup folder and the Run registry key. It then contacts amexsafekeyupdate.com to retrieve installation commands for two separate installers. VirusTotal sandbox activity associated with the sample includes downloads of ScreenConnect MSI installers from cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com and cyberrexdesign.screenconnect[.]com, with digitaldownloads[.]com listed by Huntress as a potential IOC. DigitalDownloads ScreenConnect portal Source: BleepingComputer After launching the second installer, the script uses PowerShell to search running processes and Windows services for ed630cc2c873b091, one of the rogue ScreenConnect client IDs identified by Huntress. If the identifier is found, the script considers the installation successful and sends a notification to the attackers through Telegram. The earlier script also appears designed for a different distribution campaign, with its Social Security-themed filename suggesting it may have been used in phishing attacks. It remains unclear whether the July activity and the current MSP attacks are part of the same campaign. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 1b4qibx.text: Certificate authority eMudhra has revoked eight additional intermediate CA certificates after an investigation into its recent certificate security incident found improper handling of private keys during the certificate-generation process. The new revocations bring the total number of affected intermediate CA certificates to 16, including eight previously compromised certificates whose private keys were so weak that anyone could recover them almost instantly. In a new incident report published Tuesday, eMudhra said that both sets of certificates were affected by a custom Python script used to transfer private keys between hardware security modules (HSMs) in April 2025. HSMs are devices designed to securely generate and store cryptographic keys, preventing sensitive private keys from being exposed outside the hardware. eMudhra says it developed the script to move certificate authority keys between different HSM vendors at its facilities after delays in obtaining new hardware. However, the script contained a bug that reduced eight ECDSA private keys to a single byte, making them extremely easy to recover. The same script also processed eight RSA private keys, which handled sensitive key information in the memory of the computer running the script rather than keeping it protected within the HSM. While the RSA keys were not weakened like the original eight certificates, eMudhra says it could not demonstrate that it handled them under its certificate security policies. "A re‑import performed from host process memory is not consistent with the CPS §6.2.6 and the RSA objects are therefore treated as not meeting that requirement," reads the incident report. Due to this, the company revoked the additional eight RSA intermediate CA certificates on November 7, including certificates used to issue TLS and code-signing certificates. Some of the affected RSA intermediates had been actively issuing certificates since May 2026, with the last certificate issued on November 3. eMudhra says the affected customer certificates have also been replaced or migrated. The investigation also found that an earlier problem in June 2025 could have revealed the flaw more than a year before it was discovered by a security researcher known as "Wayne." At that time, eMudhra detected certificate revocation lists (CRLs) signed with private keys that did not match the corresponding CA certificates. The company fixed the issue by signing the revocation lists with the matching keys but did not investigate why the problem occurred. The new report confirms this was an early warning sign of the faulty key-generation process that went undetected until October 2026. The investigation also found that eMudhra did not verify the strength of generated private keys or check that the keys used for certification matched those originally created in the HSM. Major browsers blocked compromised certificates As BleepingComputer previously reported, the incident was first disclosed on October 17, when a security researcher named Wayne discovered that eight eMudhra intermediate CA private keys could be recovered by testing just 256 possible values. Major browsers and operating systems trusted the compromised certificates, potentially allowing attackers to forge certificates for legitimate websites and intercept encrypted communications. Mozilla, Google, Apple, and other software vendors subsequently released protections to block the compromised certificates. Microsoft also released out-of-band Windows updates on October 26 to remove trust in affected eMudhra certificate trust chains on systems that could not receive automatic certificate trust updates. Following the incident, eMudhra announced that it would exit the publicly trusted TLS certificate business and transition its remaining customers to another provider. The company says it plans to stop issuing certificates under its remaining G1 hierarchy by November 16. eMudhra has also commissioned an independent review by KPMG, with findings expected by December 4, to identify improvements to its certificate management and key-generation procedures. The company says it has not detected any evidence that the compromised keys were used maliciously. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 16iakw7.text: Notion, the digital workspace platform, disclosed that a security breach at its AI infrastructure provider, Fireworks AI, exposed Notion AI chat transcripts in a small number of workspaces. The disclosure comes shortly after Fireworks AI confirmed that an attacker accessed its development environment via a third-party cloud provider on October 23 and compromised resource metadata, billing information, model weights, and datasets for some customers. Fireworks AI experienced another breach in early October, when hackers accessed environment variables containing API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts. Notion learned about the exposed chat transcripts after receiving an alert from Fireworks on November 2 about an exposed dataset that contained only synthetic test data. Notion responded by cutting off traffic to Fireworks, deleting all data from the vendor’s systems, and halting training runs by November 3. However, Fireworks confirmed on November 8 that customer data had been accessed, including that of Notion users. Notion is a cloud-based workspace used for note-taking, document creation, internal wikis, project management, and task tracking. It includes an AI assistant that can answer questions, summarize content, and help draft text. Fireworks AI enables Notion to run some of the open-weight models available through Notion AI and analyze stored conversations for Insights, a feature that gives workspace administrators visibility into how their teams use AI. The exposed transcripts came from the Insights dataset specifically, which has now been disabled. “Upon analysis of the dataset Fireworks AI gave us on November 8, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were unattributable,” Notion stated in an update. "Unattributable means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results.” Notion has also published a FAQ page about the incident, highlighting that Fireworks had contractually committed to zero data retention for Notion data. According to the company, less than 1% of its users are impacted by the incident. Potentially affected workspace owners should review the data through Security incident review in Notion’s desktop web interface and share a link with members that lets them download their own transcripts. Notion advises affected users to rotate any passwords, API keys, or other credentials entered into affected chats. If neither a user nor their workspace owner has received a notice, Notion says no action is needed for now, and they are most likely not part of the impacted subset. 7ocoy1.text: The U.S. accused three men of orchestrating attacks across Europe on behalf of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), including a London arson incident that was recorded for propaganda. An indictment unsealed Tuesday says the broader campaign, targeting Jewish and American sites, included attacks on synagogues in Belgium, the Netherlands and London, and U.S. bank buildings in Amsterdam and Paris. It also included a stabbing in London that left two Jewish men seriously injured. Prosecutors say the same network later plotted to attack RAF Fairford, a British air base used by U.S. bombers, with vans and what the plotters intended to be explosives. During the attack one suspect directed the vans toward the base by phone from Iran, while another, already jailed in New York, relayed coded instructions through calls with relatives. The superseding indictment adds two defendants to a case against Mohammad al-Saadi, an alleged commander of the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kataib Hezbollah who has been jailed in New York since May. The additional defendants are Mohsen Mohajeri, whom prosecutors identify as an IRGC operative, and Mohammed Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi who once lived in Britain. Both are at large and believed to be in Iran. All three face terrorism charges carrying potential life sentences. Prosecutors say that recording the attempted attacks for propaganda was an essential part of the network’s operations. The indictment includes images of them directing attacks from a room in Iraq, as well as recordings of instructions given to the attackers. During an arson attack on a Jewish charity's building in London in April, al-Hassani told the attacker to “light one in your hand,” “light it” and “throw the fourth one,” according to the indictment. The attack was streamed over FaceTime and projected onto a large screen with the militia’s logo. The IRGC operative filmed the proceedings and the men directing it. Two days earlier, al-Hassani allegedly directed another arson attack on Iran International, a London-based media organization that has repeatedly faced attacks from the Iranian regime. Again over a video call, al-Hassani told the attacker to get close to the gate and ensure he could see what was happening on camera. During another attack on a London synagogue the following day, he urged the attacker to “light it up like a Christmas tree.” In March, when al-Saadi asked the IRGC operative Mohajeri about working with his militia on joint attacks involving drones and missiles, Mohajeri agreed and told him to “make sure to photograph a video and pictures.” The attacks were claimed by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya, or HAYI, which prosecutors describe as a front for Kataib Hezbollah and the IRGC. The group claimed about 18 attacks and attempted attacks across Europe between March and April, beginning days after the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran. HAYI also claimed that drones carrying radioactive material had targeted the Israeli Embassy in London, although police found no hazardous material after investigating the incident. Al-Saadi had received videos days earlier showing men in hazmat suits posing beside a drone that had been fitted with vials of an unspecified white powder. Hybrid Theory The new indictment gives the most detailed account yet of how the attacks were directed from afar — drawing on recordings, images and messages exchanged across several apps — and comes amid concerns over what Western authorities describe as “hybrid warfare” and “state-sponsored terrorism.” Much of the evidence comes from al-Saadi's own iPhone, which FBI agents seized after he was first detained in Turkey in May. Prosecutors say it contained recordings of FaceTime calls, raw attack footage and messages with a Kataib Hezbollah contact. FaceTime calls are end-to-end encrypted, meaning Apple cannot access their content while the calls are ongoing, however investigators were able to obtain recordings stored on al-Saadi’s seized phone. The seizure of this evidence comes amid disputes over law enforcement access to encrypted data, particularly in Europe and the United Kingdom. Apple is currently challenging a reported British demand for access to protected iCloud data, while the European Commission has outlined plans to explore technical options for lawful access to encrypted evidence. Images in the new indictment show what prosecutors say are Mohajeri and al-Hassani planning attacks while sitting in front of a laptop displaying a map of London, as well as stills from videos of the men directing attacks live. Earlier images of al-Saadi show him mingling with senior Iranian and militia commanders. These came from his phone and social media accounts, prosecutors said. The FBI linked his WhatsApp, Snapchat, Telegram and X accounts through a single phone number. Earlier filings say al-Saadi received raw footage of a bombing of a synagogue in Liège, Belgium, through Telegram and used the app to send footage of an arson attack on Jewish volunteer ambulances in London to a contact saved in his phone as a China-based media company. Prosecutors also say al-Saadi paid an undercover officer about $3,000 in cryptocurrency in April, which was related to a planned attack on a Manhattan synagogue. The nature of the transaction was not detailed, and no attack took place. In August, al-Hassani allegedly paid someone to film the perimeter of the RAF Fairford airbase, which houses U.S. military aircraft and personnel. The following month, paid associates bought vans, barrels of fuel and metal objects that could serve as shrapnel, and researched buying chemicals, according to the indictment. During the alleged attempted attack towards the end of that month, al-Hassani was described as being in frequent contact by phone with the drivers of three vans heading toward the base, directing their movements from Iran, prosecutors say. It is not clear whether he used normal voice calls or communicated via an app. At least two of the vans were turned back at a security roadblock. British authorities recovered the vehicles in the early hours of the next morning and arrested their occupants. Police said at the time they found no explosives but seized petrol. Seven people were arrested and released on bail. Apple, Snap, X and Meta, which owns WhatsApp, did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Al-Saadi's X account, which the FBI says had posted calls for revenge against Americans as early as 2020, remained online Wednesday. 1vcnzc.text: Shipping giant Maersk has confirmed that a threat actor breached systems belonging to a company it previously acquired and stole data. Ransomware group WhiteArmor claimed the attack over the weekend, threatening that it would release about 100GB of information allegedly exfiltrated from the company's logistics and supply-chain platform. Legacy system compromise The investigation into the incident is ongoing, but the shipping firm says that current evidence indicates that "no sensitive data has been disclosed." Maersk added that it does not expect disruptions to operations, and assures customers that they can continue booking and managing shipments through its systems as usual. “The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI,” Maersk states. A.P. Moller–Maersk is a Danish shipping and logistics group and one of the world’s largest container carriers by fleet capacity. The company operates ocean freighters, port terminals, warehouses, and air and land transport services across 130 countries. It has 700 container ships, roughly 13.5% of the global fleet capacity, 60 terminals in 35 countries, and employs 100,000 people. Last year, Maersk reported $54 billion in revenue and $2.9 billion in net profit. Maersk said the incident has been isolated, but did not share details about the affected system, the compromised data types, or when the intrusion occurred. BleepingComputer reached out to Maersk with additional questions, but we have not heard back as of publishing. Ransomware gang claims 100GB data theft Over the weekend, the WhiteArmor ransomware gang listed Maersk on its data leak site and publicly asked for a ransom payment of $5million. "Your contract-logistics arm, the former LF Logistics, runs fulfilment for many of the world's largest consumer brands. Five million dollars is roughly four hours of that EBITDA," the threat actor said. "You have 30 days to contact us and pay USD 5,000,000 in bitcoin," reads WhiteArmor's public message. WhiteArmor claims to hold approximately 100 GB of data allegedly stolen from Maersk's OCF/LF Logistics platform, which the group is using to support its extortion demands. In 2022, Maersk acquired LF Logistics, the original developer of the OCF/LF Logistics platform, from the Li & Fung Group. 1kkzi6q.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 11, 2026Vulnerability / Software Security Zoom has released software updates to address two security flaws impacting Zoom Workplace for Windows, including a critical bug that could result in privilege escalation on affected systems. The vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-108186 (CVSS score: 9.6) - An improper input validation vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated user to conduct an escalation of privilege via network access. CVE-2026-108187 (CVSS score: 8.1) - An origin validation vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated user to conduct an escalation of privilege via network access. Successful exploitation of either of the shortcomings could permit remote attackers to escalate privileges without requiring any special permissions or access. While CVE-2026-108187 affects Zoom Workplace for Windows before version 7.1.5, CVE-2026-108186 impacts versions starting from 7.1.0 and before 7.1.8. 1sej7d.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a campaign in which an emerging agentic penetration testing platform called AntiFox has been used to steal Amazon Web Services (AWS) credentials and pivot laterally into compromised environments. "In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments," Arctic Wolf Labs said in a report shared with The Hacker News. The activity has been observed chaining together web exploitation and web shell deployment to facilitate configuration discovery, credential validation, cloud-service enumeration, secret access, and storage operations. AntiFox, available for download from GitHub, has been described as an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven autonomous penetration testing platform. As of writing, the project has been forked 251 times and starred 474 times. On its README page, the project maintainer states - Given an authorized target, a planner / worker / main-agent multi-agent system runs the full engagement over a dual-graph core (a global asset graph + a per-task exploration graph) — recon → attack-surface discovery → exploitation → finding capture → report delivery — fully observable, interactive, and deliverable Unlike most automated pentest tools that are "great at discovery, but stop at discovery," AntiFox puts its weight on delivery — turning what the AI finds into a report that an engineer can understand, reproduce, back with evidence, and hand straight to the client. According to Arctic Wolf, some of the initial access activity is associated with a compromised internet-facing Internet Information Services (IIS) application. The access is then leveraged to create an ASPX web shell using "w3wp.exe," the IIS worker process, and run operating system commands to perform the following actions - Run PowerShell commands to locate web.config files and configuration backups Read application settings and database connection strings Enumerate debug and error-log directories Attempts to connect to an internal production database using a credential extracted from the application configuration Copy configuration and log files into a web-accessible upload directory "On a compromised IIS server, commands run through w3wp.exe identified the execution context with whoami, enumerated the application directory, checked permissions with icacls, and tested the ability to write files into the web root," Arctic Wolf said. "The creation of an ASPX web shell by w3wp.exe, followed by command execution through the same IIS worker process, suggests compromise through the affected web application." The precise vulnerability used to achieve code execution on the IIS server is not known. In other attacks, the threat actor is said to have started with a valid AWS credential obtained through as-yet-undetermined means. AntiFox Demo Specifically, this involved abusing valid IAM identities to validate credentials and enumerate dozens of services, including IAM, EC2, S3, Lambda, Secrets Manager, KMS, RDS, ECS, EKS, Redshift, Athena, Glue, Systems Manager, API Gateway, CloudWatch, CloudFormation, DynamoDB, and Amazon Bedrock. While a majority of these authenticated cross-service API requests ended up with an "AccessDenied" error, some of the discovery and secret-access operations were successful, according to the cybersecurity company. In at least some instances, the activity has been observed progressing beyond Secrets Manager enumeration to a successful GetSecretValue request against a production secret. Elsewhere, a valid AWS identity was used for S3 discovery and object operations via API calls. "Agentic frameworks such as these make penetration testing techniques more accessible to threat actors, while increasing the speed and consistency with which these techniques can be applied in live attacks," Arctic Wolf said. The Rise of AI Tools in Cyber Attacks The disclosure comes as threat actors are increasingly weaponizing AI-powered penetration testing tools like ARTEX to conduct broad-scale attacks across the world, enabling them to automate various stages of an intrusion with minimal human intervention. The integration of AI has allowed adversaries, both large and small, to adapt established tradecraft and deploy them at machine speed, making it possible to progress from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from an Azure Key Vault in five minutes. Earlier this week, VECERT disclosed details of a campaign dubbed Operation Ghost-Campus orchestrated by a Chinese threat actor that uses AI agents to maintain perpetual, cost-free access to large language models (LLMs) and eventually perform automated academic fraud and steal data belonging to over 5,000 students enrolled at the Fengxian Campus. "The agent industrializes the creation of accounts on the search engine fofa.info, scans the global cyberspace for misconfigured servers, extracts API keys for OpenAI and DeepSeek, automatically verifies their financial balances, and injects them into the attacker's development environment," VECERT said. "This stolen computing power fuels an interactive GoTTY terminal ('Pi — AI Coding Assistant') and, by extension, provides intelligence to the scripts that sustain academic fraud bots ('heartbeat' bots) and extractors of financial data and personally identifiable information (PII) belonging to thousands of students at the Fengxian Campus." According to data from Censys, there are 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console as of November 4, 2026, with most of them located in the U.S., Hong Kong, China, Japan, Singapore, and South Korea. However, it's worth noting that not every instance is necessarily malicious in nature. In a separate report, Check Point Research said it identified 2,557 systems that hosted ARTEX, including 10 misconfigured instances exposing their full databases. "In many observed cases, ARTEX required remarkably little interaction from its operators once an objective had been established," Check Point said. "Rather than continuously directing attacks step by step, operators frequently issued a goal and left the agent fleet to work toward it. Human interactions were largely limited to checking progress, asking whether a target had been compromised or occasionally adjusting priorities." The vast majority of the attacks are designed to siphon cryptocurrency, steal Apple code-signing certificates, compromise gaming accounts, and conduct denial-of-service (DoS) attacks against gambling websites. The activity has been found to exploit vulnerabilities related to weak or hard-coded passwords, missing authentication, insecure direct object references, and remote code execution. In the campaign targeting Apple code-signing certificates, ARTEX agents searched compromised systems for certificate databases, followed by validating the stolen certificates by checking passwords, private keys, Apple revocation status, expiration dates, and associated provisioning profiles. Ultimately, the activity is estimated to have harvested more than 300 certificates and their passwords, out of which three certificates passed the full validation process and could be used to sign arbitrary iOS applications. The biggest change brought by agentic hacking to the cyber threat landscape is scale and speed, Check Point cautioned, as a cybercriminal with limited technical skills can task AI agents with investigating a number of targets in parallel and exploiting them using known and zero-day vulnerabilities with less manual effort. "Its relevance to us lies in its scale, speed and persistence," CERT-EU said in an alert. "ARTEX can test large numbers of low-complexity misconfigurations, including those a human tester would notice but not have time to check, and it can work through long attack chains without the fatigue that limits manual testing." "The same is true of complex payload crafting. Exploitation paths that need carefully tailored payloads often take more effort than the severity of the finding justifies, so a manual assessment may leave them untested." Tools like AntiFox and ARTEX are part of a broader set of about 45 open-source agentic attack frameworks that are engineered to connect to an LLM and can act on outputs autonomously. They fall under five broad categories - Network kill chain capable of end-to-end reconnaissance, exploitation, and post-exploitation: PentAGI, RedAmon, and DarkMoon Web-app and API: Strix, Shannon, and PentestGPT C2-integrated: Sage, echidna, Pojun, and FORANG Harnesses: RAPTOR, CyberStrike, cyber-harness, Nebula and Cybermes Research prototypes: Incalmo, hackingBuddyGPT, VulnBot, HackSynth, AutoPT, and Ares "Each framework has public source code and wires a model into a loop that runs tools and acts on their output," GitGuardian said. "Agentic AI pentesting tools hand their agent a shell and web access, so the model can assemble a pipeline at runtime. A GitHub search, a scanner download, and a found key passed to the next call are all one prompt away, even though none of it ships in the repository."

fl088x.text: Attackers are using Alibaba Cloud to host self-managed instances of AntiFox, an open-source agentic penetration testing platform, to target web services and AWS environments. The infrastructure hosting AntiFox was used for various malicious activities, including vulnerability exploitation, webshell deployment, credential validation, configuration discovery, and AWS secret harvesting. Initially created as a fork of ARTEX 0.1.1, AntiFox has a Chinese-language interface and lets users deploy AI agents and automate common penetration-testing tasks, such as mapping exposed services and probing target endpoints for vulnerabilities. Security researchers at Arctic Wolf observed malicious AntiFox-linked infrastructure hosted on Alibaba Cloud using valid AWS identities, including IAM users and, in some cases, assumed EC2 roles, to make authenticated requests to Amazon Web Services APIs. “In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments,” Arctic Wolf says. One case highlighted in the report involved deploying an ASPX webshell on an internet-exposed IIS server, executing OS commands, accessing application settings and database connection strings, and copying configuration and log files to a web-accessible directory. The attacker also used valid IAM credentials and EC2 roles to probe Amazon Web Services (AWS) endpoints. In one intrusion, they cycled through multiple identities and made hundreds of API requests in about 30 minutes, the researchers note. Although most of these attempts were blocked, the attacker was successful in some cases and obtained production secrets. In a separate incident, the attackers used a valid AWS identity to read, copy, and delete S3 objects. Arctic Wolf's report includes hunting guidance and recommendations for defenders that include correlating IIS webshell activity with unusual AWS access and reviewing successful API calls within bursts of denials. The researchers also recommend revoking affected AWS sessions and keys and rotating credentials exposed through application files. The AntiFox findings follow recent attacks involving ARTEX AI, another agentic penetration-testing framework developed in China that went closed-source after it was used in attacks on South Korean banks. CrowdStrike also linked ARTEX to a cyberespionage campaign in which the Chinese hacking group Vapor Panda targeted more than 200 organizations across 14 countries. For now, AntiFox remains available on GitHub, where it has been updated to version 2.0, which improves how the tool documents and reports findings. Its publishers prohibit using the tool against live systems, in real-world penetration tests or security exercises, or for destructive or illegal activity, but they do not describe any technical controls that enforce those restrictions. gezkpi.text: For years, eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) has been one of the most celebrated technologies in the Linux kernel. It lets developers run sandboxed programs inside the kernel without writing kernel modules, while powering everything from network monitoring to security tooling. Linux is extremely popular in production servers and giants like Google, Cloudflare, and Meta rely on it daily. The same eBPF capabilities that are attractive for defenders, however, can be a powerful weapon in the hands of attackers. Flare’s research found underground forum posts sharing eBPF rootkit code and step-by-step tutorials. One Russian-language post described how to build an implant with process hiding and packet-triggered activation, and included screenshots the author presented as demonstrations. What Makes eBPF Dangerous? Traditional Linux rootkits typically rely on loadable kernel modules (LKMs) to hook system calls and hide malicious activity. These are well-understood by defenders, and most EDR solutions watch for suspicious module loads. eBPF, however, behaves in a different way. An eBPF malware can hook into kernel functions, observe system calls, or inspect and modify network traffic using the same kernel-supported bpf() interface as legitimate tools like Cilium. Its programs run without loading a kernel module, so a routine lsmod check can miss them. The challenge for defenders is determining who loaded the program and what it does. The Next Linux Rootkit Is Already Being Discussed Underground eBPF rootkits are moving from conference talks to underground forum tutorials, and by the time one loads on a host, it’s built to evade your usual checks. Flare monitors forums, marketplaces, and paste sites in real time, so your team sees new tooling, exploits, and chatter early enough to track eBPF threats. Free 2-Week Trial From Classic BPF Backdoors to eBPF Rootkits The first major wake-up call came in 2022 when PwC and Elastic Security Labs documented BPFDoor, a passive Linux backdoor attributed to a Chinese threat actor tracked as Red Menshen. The BPFDoor sample Elastic analyzed used a classic BPF socket filter to recognize specially crafted TCP, UDP, or ICMP packets. Once triggered, it could open a reverse shell or redirect traffic to the implant. PwC discovered the malware in 2021, and public reporting in 2022 described activity targeting organizations in the Middle East and Asia. Around the same time, Intezer and BlackBerry jointly disclosed Symbiote, a different flavor of Linux malware that weaponizes BPF for stealth. Rather than running as a standalone process, Symbiote uses the dynamic linker to preload a malicious shared library into affected processes. The library intercepts calls to setsockopt() that attach classic BPF filters via SO_ATTACH_FILTER and prepends its own filter instructions to conceal selected traffic from packet capture. Public research had already demonstrated offensive uses of eBPF. In 2021, researchers presented ebpfkit at Black Hat USA and DEF CON. TripleCross combines syscall hooks with XDP and traffic control programs to support library injection, execution hijacking, concealment, and command and control. Boopkit uses getdents64 hooks to hide directory entries. An already installed implant can be triggered remotely in two documented ways, one involving a malformed TCP SYN and the other using ordinary TCP connections. Lastly, in October 2025, Synacktiv reported LinkPro after investigating a compromise that began with an exposed Jenkins server. LinkPro used eBPF programs to hide activity on the host and activate the backdoor when it received a specially crafted packet. Underground Adoption: From Research to Weaponization Security researchers and state-sponsored threat actors have explored how eBPF can be used to build rootkits. Flare’s recent research found underground forum posts sharing code and step-by-step tutorials, showing that these techniques now circulate beyond academic papers and security conferences. On the Russian-language Duty Free forum, a user published a tutorial on building an eBPF rootkit and cited BPFDoor and Symbiote as influences. Screenshot from Flare's platform showing the title and outline of an eBPF rootkit tutorial posted on the Duty Free forum. Sign up for the free trial to access if you aren’t already a customer. The guide includes source code and screenshots that the author presents as demonstrations. It describes how to activate the implant with a TCP SYN packet with a specific window size, hide processes by hooking getdents64, and encrypt command-and-control traffic with AES-256-GCM. The guide also describes using XDP to inspect incoming plaintext HTTP traffic and drop packets that match a list of 43 IP addresses the author associates with antivirus vendors. Flare also identified 10 related Pastebin posts containing XDP packet-processing code and timing thresholds expressed in microseconds. eBPF Beyond Rootkits Flare also found exploit code circulating across multiple platforms. The most frequently reposted exploit (at least six platforms) in the dataset targeted CVE-2017-16995, a 2017 Linux BPF verifier flaw involving incorrect sign extension. Alongside the older eBPF exploits, researchers discovered some fresh exploits. One example is an unverified Linux local privilege escalation PoC targeting kTLS and eBPF sockmaps. The proof-of-concept attempts to corrupt the page cache for /etc/passwd and inject an account with UID 0. Its claim of compatibility with all kernels from 4.18 onward is incorrect. Upstream Linux 4.18 lacks a BPF helper the code calls. Successful privilege escalation on Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04 has not been verified. In one exploit sample we reviewed, the author credited Claude in a source code comment with generating the BPF instructions. Why Detection Is So Hard The fundamental challenge is that eBPF-based threats operate through a legitimate kernel interface. Unlike a rogue kernel module, an eBPF program passes through the kernel’s built-in verifier and a malicious program that passes verification looks, to the kernel, like any other approved program. Detection today focuses on monitoring bpf() syscalls, tracking loaded programs via bpftool, and watching for suspicious attachment points on sensitive syscalls like getdents64 and execve. But these are reactive measures, and attackers have the advantage of operating through the kernel’s own sanctioned mechanisms. What Defenders Should Do Organizations running Linux infrastructure should take eBPF threats seriously: Audit loaded eBPF programs regularly with bpftool prog list. Know what’s supposed to be there. Restrict eBPF access via kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled=1 and limit CAP_BPF / CAP_NET_ADMIN. Monitor for magic packets — several eBPF backdoors activate via specific TCP flags or window sizes. Patch aggressively — BPF verifier bugs are a recurring vulnerability class, and weaponized exploits appear fast. Watch for unexpected XDP programs on network interfaces. Gather fresh threat intelligence – stay up to date on new attack vectors, tools and techniques which may help you tailor new detections and enforcement to block eBPF- based malware. The Bottom Line eBPF rootkits represent a genuine evolution in Linux threats as their implants can evade checks focused on loaded kernel modules. LinkPro went further by trying to hide its eBPF programs from bpftool prog list. Investigators could still see associated BPF maps and links, illustrating why defenders should compare multiple sources of host telemetry. Flare found underground posts sharing source code and instructions for hiding processes and activating an implant with a crafted packet. Synacktiv documented both techniques in its investigation of LinkPro, giving defenders a concrete example of how they can appear in an intrusion. Learn more by signing up for our free trial. jb0rdv.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 11, 2026Cyber Attack / Ransomware Threat actors have been observed targeting Qlik Sense servers to unsuccessfully deliver PowerShell reverse shell commands against multiple environments in October 2026. Cynet's CyOps and Research teams said they identified the suspicious activity in October 2026 against several E.U.-based customers within a narrow window of just over three minutes. The activity has been found to share some level of overlap with a November 2023 campaign documented by Arctic Wolf in which threat actors linked to the CACTUS ransomware operation likely weaponized then-newly-disclosed flaws in Qlik Sense to obtain initial access to target environments. The vulnerabilities in question, which were patched by Qlik Sense in August and September 2023, impact Qlik Sense Enterprise for Windows - CVE-2023-41265 (CVSS score: 9.6) - An HTTP tunneling vulnerability that could lead to privilege escalation and allow an attacker to execute HTTP requests on the backend server hosting the repository application. CVE-2023-41266 (CVSS score: 8.2) - A path traversal vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to generate an anonymous session and perform HTTP requests to unauthorized endpoints. CVE-2023-48365 (CVSS score: 9.6) - An unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability that stems from improper validation of HTTP headers, allowing an attacker to elevate their privilege by tunneling HTTP requests and execute HTTP requests on the backend server. It's worth noting that CVE-2023-48365 (aka DoubleQlik) is an incomplete fix for CVE-2023-41265. In November 2023 CACTUS ransomware campaign, threat actors were observed exploiting the flaws to establish a foothold and download additional payloads to establish persistence and remote control by deploying ManageEngine Unified Endpoint Management and Security (UEMS), AnyDesk, and Plink. The latest activity detected by Cynet involves the use of a PowerShell command containing a one-line reverse shell that connects to "45.115.26[.]23" on port 4455. The exact vulnerability exploited to break into Qlik Sense servers is currently not known. "The command was executed under scheduler.exe, resembling the 2023 Cactus Qlik intrusions," the cybersecurity company said. Although attempts to spawn the reverse shell were blocked, Cynet's testing of the reverse shell in a controlled environment has revealed that the interactive communication channel is used to conduct reconnaissance and deliver a PowerShell script for enabling persistence. This is achieved by means of a Windows Go reverse shell that connects to "45.115.26[.]23:4456." The backdoor is then used to look for actively running processes related to Apache ActiveMQ. On Linux, the malware also attempts to collect system information and read "/etc/shadow" and "/etc/passwd" files. A second variant of the PowerShell script attempts to install OpenSSH and creates a scheduled task named "WinUpdCheck" that launches a PowerShell reverse shell written to "C:\ProgramData\ssh\winc.ps1" at five-minute intervals. "If sshd remained unavailable, it downloaded OpenSSH-Win64.zip from the staging server, extracted it, and ran install-sshd.ps1," Cynet said. "It set sshd to automatic startup, started the service, and added an inbound firewall rule for TCP 22. The archive was a legitimate OpenSSH package reused by the operator." Further analysis of the infrastructure has uncovered an exposed directory ("45.115.26[.]23:8012") consisting of a custom Go backdoor for Windows, SSH persistence scripts, an ActiveMQ exploit for CVE-2023-46604, and a modified public Veeam toolchain for CVE-2024-40711, indicating the threat actor is possibly laying the groundwork for broader attacks.

fuhcoz.text: Poland temporarily shut down a government platform used by citizens and businesses to access public services after detecting and stopping a cyberattack, officials said Tuesday. The attack targeted ePUAP, a nationwide system that allows users to submit official documents, communicate with government agencies and complete administrative procedures online. Polish Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said security teams responded immediately to the incident and were working to restore the platform's full functionality. "The cyberattack on the state ePUAP system was detected and stopped," Gawkowski said in a social media post. The minister said the infrastructure of Poland's Central Information Technology Center, the government agency responsible for maintaining key digital services, including ePUAP, remained secure. Officials said the ePUAP platform was taken offline as a precaution rather than because of damage caused by the attack. "It's not that the system was somehow compromised or its operation was disrupted by this attack," Marek Gieorgica, a spokesperson for the Digital Affairs Ministry, told Polish news agency PAP. "We simply disabled it as a precautionary measure." Authorities have not disclosed how the attack was carried out or who was responsible. There has been no public confirmation that hackers gained access to government systems or stole sensitive information. The ministry has not provided a timeline for restoring the platform, saying services will resume once security specialists complete their work. According to a notice on the government's website, ePUAP electronic mailboxes remain unavailable to citizens and public institutions. The disruption could also temporarily affect the Trusted Profile digital identity system, which allows people to access public services and electronically sign official documents. Poland has faced repeated cyberattacks targeting government institutions, critical infrastructure and private companies in recent months. In October, Polish online invoicing provider Fakturownia reported a data breach that may have exposed information belonging to its users, customers and business partners. In September, hackers also stole data from Qbusoft, a Polish healthcare software provider, following a separate breach involving medical technology company MyDr. Polish authorities said the MyDr incident potentially affected information relating to about 19 million people and roughly 12,000 healthcare organizations. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. 1x0xuk3.text: Fourteen governments participating in the Pall Mall Process, a diplomatic effort led by Britain and France to rein in the global spyware industry, adopted their first guidelines for commercial hacking businesses on Wednesday. The French Foreign Ministry said the guidelines, aimed at addressing abuses associated with the proliferation of commercial cyber intrusion capabilities (CCICs), set out “the first global standard of responsible conduct.” “Access to certain capabilities once reserved for a handful of specialized government agencies has gradually widened: any actor can now buy ‘off the shelf’ the ability to silently penetrate a phone,” the ministry said. While it acknowledged those tools have been used in intelligence operations and to tackle organized crime, the ministry warned they “have also been implicated in surveillance campaigns targeting journalists, political officials, activists or businesses.” The guidelines are non-binding and endorsed by governments rather than industry organizations. They call on businesses that develop, sell or finance CCICs to vet their customers, establish technical safeguards against misuse and to maintain systems for monitoring and reporting abuses. Companies should halt sales and support when serious misuse is a credible risk, according to the text, and are asked to “consider” remedies for victims of human rights abuses. There are no penalties for non-compliance and enforcement pressure is expected to come from governments which buy the tools and license their export. The point of the industry guidelines is “to disincentivise irresponsible activity across the market for CCICs; improve transparency for regulators, vendors and customers; and provide clarity for businesses operating both within and peripherally to the industry,” said the British Foreign Office. The guidelines were endorsed at the Pall Mall initiative’s third conference, attended by representatives from 43 countries. Fewer than half signed up to endorse them, with signatories including the United Kingdom and France, alongside the United States, Germany, Italy and Japan. The guidelines “are voluntary in nature,” the ministry said. “They do not create new international legal obligations and do not call into question uses that states consider legitimate in the fields of national security, defense, the fight against organized crime or cybersecurity. “A voluntary code is not, however, an optional code: one’s word, given before one’s peers, one’s industries and one’s citizens, is a commitment.” The Pall Mall Process has faced persistent challenges since its launch in London in 2024. While that event drew large technology and cybersecurity firms, it did not feature the controversial businesses whose products had been linked to abuses. A year later, participants raised concerns that the initiative lacks the ability to actually change how these tools are traded and used. Some noted that Britain and France were seeking to restrict other states’ access to these tools while championing their own spyware industries. Last year’s conference produced the first code of practice for governments, but no agreement on how to influence company behavior. Twenty-seven countries have since signed the code. It is not clear why the remaining 15 did not endorse the new code on Wednesday. The ministry said participants would continue their work as “artificial intelligence, the growing automation of certain functions and the emergence of new business models” raise new questions for governments and companies. ot7ij1.text: N-able released hotfixes to address zero-day bugs affecting its N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform, which were publicly disclosed over the weekend and forced it to take vulnerable hosted environments offline. This follows N-able's decision to take all hosted N-central environments offline across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific regions until it could patch them against potential attacks targeting the zero-day flaws in the wild. "N-able is actively responding to non-responsible communication of critical vulnerabilities in N-central late Sunday night, November 8, found by an independent researcher," N-able told BleepingComputer on Monday. "As a precautionary measure, we took our Hosted N-central environment offline today, November 9, and provided guidance to customers operating on-premises N-central servers to temporarily take their servers offline until further notice." N-central lets IT departments and managed service providers (MSPs) monitor, manage, and maintain client networks and devices from a centralized web-based console. N-able has now released N-central 2026.4 HF2 with security patches and technology updates for some of the leaked zero-days, including "the most critical" vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-125883 - Multiple XXE Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-125878 - Multiple OGNL Injection vulnerabilities CVE-2026-125879 - Local privilege escalation to root via nable-writable syslog-ng config CVE-2026-125880 - Stored XSS via MMS3 patch metadata (admin context) CVE-2026-125881 - Schema-hint SSRF via service import schema validation CVE-2026-125882 - RCE via file repository upload path traversal (Credit Nate Fair, Sprocket Security) CVE-2026-91000 - Insecure IPC Channels lead to local privilege escalation In a Tuesday update, N-able said that all hosted N-central servers (NCODs) across all regions have now been successfully upgraded and advised and "strongly" recommended that all N-central On-Premises customers upgrade their installations to the newly released version "as soon as possible." "Customers should follow the published upgrade guidance carefully before restoring normal access to their N-central environment. Earlier incident guidance advised On-Premises customers to keep their N-central servers offline while remediation was being developed," it said. While N-able has yet to flag these flaws as exploited in the wild, threat intelligence company Defused said on Tuesday that attackers have already started scanning the Internet for vulnerable systems and warned admins to take N-central servers offline immediately. "During the past 24 hours, we have observed probing of N-able N-central for the 0-days that were dropped publicly yesterday," Defused said. "We have seen opening of anonymous agent sessions, pulling appliance config and hitting the remote control endpoint without auth. These pathways are part of the 0-day exploit surface." Internet security nonprofit Shadowserver reports that just over 148 N-central servers are currently exposed online, a sharp decrease from the 1,338 it detected on Monday. Internet-exposed N-central servers (Shadowserver) Disclosed after previous reports were allegedly ignored Security researcher Sean Bales disclosed the vulnerabilities late Sunday, November 8, and published a GitHub repository called Able2Shell containing proof-of-concept exploits for the flaws. Bales said the zero-day bugs affect N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31, a pre-release version of the software, and believes that most (if not all) of the flaws also affect earlier versions. The disclosed vulnerabilities include remote code execution (RCE), authentication bypasses, credential disclosure, arbitrary file writes, directory traversal, XML external entity (XXE) injection, and cross-site scripting (XSS) flaws. The security researcher also demoed a critical unauthenticated XXE-to-RCE exploit chain that abuses N-central's service-import functionality to steal a trusted local session, reset the targeted account's password, and execute commands on the server as the nable user. Attackers could also use this exploit to create a Default Administrator account with attacker-controlled credentials, which provides them rogue admin access to the N-central management interface, as shown in the video demo embedded below. Bales told BleepingComputer that he released the N-central zero-days without notifying N-able because the company allegedly failed to patch vulnerabilities (including two unrelated remote code execution bugs and a privilege-escalation flaw) he reported in a different N-able product about five to six months ago. When asked about Bales' allegations regarding the previously disclosed security issues, N-able did not address the questions and instead responded with a statement about the N-central security incident and precautionary shutdown.
