1ycxb7y.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 10, 2026Vulnerability / Mobile Security An iMessage flaw could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages, Apple said yesterday, and it released updates to fix it. The updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined. As of today, other updates released yesterday for the iPhone XS, XS Max and XR, the iPad (7th generation) and some Apple Watch models do not list either fix. The company's notes also do not say whether either flaw has been exploited, what an attacker would need, whether group members would see someone who joined this way, or whether every member must update to be protected. The updates that fix the iMessage flaws also fix a flaw in Google's Brotli compression library. The notes do not mention any attacks using that flaw. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 27. The flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat is tracked as CVE-2026-113961. It is an authorization issue that the updates fix through improved validation. The flaw involving earlier messages is CVE-2026-113960. Which Updates Carry the Fixes Each operating system version got its own update. The security advisory for iOS and iPadOS 27.2.1 describes all three flaws. The security releases list links to the notes for every update. The iOS 18.7.12 notes and the watchOS 26.6.1 notes list other security fixes but not the iMessage or Brotli fixes. The company does not say whether devices on those versions are affected by the three flaws. Its notes also offer no workaround for anyone who cannot update right away. The Brotli flaw, CVE-2026-111497, is an out-of-bounds write in the library's decoder that could let malicious input corrupt memory. CISA's catalog entry for the Brotli decoder flaw names Google's Brotli as the affected product and says different products could use the component. All nine updates fix Bluetooth and AirPlay flaws. Two could allow a malicious Bluetooth device, or an attacker within Bluetooth range, to pair with a device without user interaction. The notes do not say what a paired device could then do. Two others could let an attacker bypass the limit on pairing code attempts, one from Bluetooth range and one from the same network. Another could let an attacker in Bluetooth range corrupt process memory.

1wdf40n.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 10, 2026Cyber Espionage / Malware The Russia-aligned state-sponsored threat actor known as Turla (aka Snake) is wielding a previously undocumented cyber espionage toolset called Cereal that's used to break into victims' Microsoft Exchange servers with an aim to surreptitiously collect emails. According to an ESET report shared with The Hacker News ahead of publication, the sophisticated and modular tool is designed for long-term intelligence gathering and has been observed against two governmental entities in Kazakhstan and Romania in late 2025. "The Cereal toolset is a carefully constructed instrument for long-term, stealthy cyber espionage," the Slovakian cybersecurity company said. "It leaves little on disk, avoids external infrastructure that could be discovered and blocked, and conceals itself within legitimate Exchange processes." "The Cereal toolset demonstrates that, for Turla, Exchange servers are not just mail servers – they are durable collection points, internal execution hubs, and a suitable environment for hiding sophisticated .NET tradecraft." The toolset is a collection of interconnected components that are capable of running on Microsoft Exchange servers, receiving commands, executing them in memory, mapping the infected network, and harvesting emails of interest. The initial access vector used to deliver the malware is unknown, although the group is known to conduct spear-phishing, watering hole, and ISP-level adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) attacks. Cereal gets its name from the fact that the tools make extensive use of serialization, which refers to the process of converting a data structure or an object's state into a format that can be easily stored, transmitted, and reconstructed. A number of aspects make the malware stand apart - Absence of an external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, instead abusing a compromised Exchange server for this purpose. Sending commands in the form of separate, compiled .NET programs. Using an automated email collection module, which is injected into legitimate Microsoft Exchange processes and is engineered to manipulate the email transport pipeline. The combination of these techniques shows that the threat actor possesses a deep understanding of the internal workings of Microsoft Exchange, ESET added. The Cereal framework consists of eight moving parts that work together to provide the attackers with access to sensitive email data - CerealRunner, which is deployed by the operator and serves as a pathway for dropping additional components, including CerealLoader, CerealSprinter, CerealIron, and CerealMoth. CerealLoader, which loads and runs a .NET assembly from an encrypted file on disk, leading to the execution of CerealSprinter. CerealSprinter, which functions similarly to CerealRunner and is used to decrypt and run CerealNeuron, CerealHermit, and CerealBox. CerealIron, an injector that makes it possible to load and run .NET assemblies from non .NET processes. CerealMoth, which receives an assembly and a method name as inputs, loads the assembly, and runs the specified method. CerealNeuron, a passive backdoor that runs on a compromised Exchange Server and listens for incoming web requests on paths that appear like regular Exchange traffic to execute assemblies contained in CerealRunner binaries. CerealHermit, a variant of CerealNeuron that reads commands from encrypted files on disk and has no network functionality of its own. CerealBox, which is the email harvesting module that processes, filters, and collects email messages by injecting itself into the Exchange transport service ("EdgeTransport.exe"). Upon gaining visibility into the email flow, the malware looks for messages containing DOC, DOCX, or PDF attachments, and matches at least one of many hard-coded lists with sender addresses, recipient addresses, subject lines, or attachment names. Emails that meet the filtering criteria are compressed, encrypted, and staged in files on disk, after which they are exfiltrated and deleted via CerealNeuron commands. In the attack aimed at the Romanian government organization, CerealBox is said to have been configured to gather emails involving NATO and European Union institutional addresses, a pattern that aligns with Russia's strategic priorities. The commands delivered as compiled .NET programs are handled by CerealRunner, which unpacks and executes the payloads in memory and then sends the results back to CerealNeuron for subsequent exfiltration to the threat actor in encrypted format. The commands support retrieving mailboxes or specific messages; queuing Active Directory for computers, users, groups, and DNS records; running Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) queries; extracting LSA Secrets; listing volume snapshots; and performing file operations. "The sheer volume of near-identical binaries, each compiled for a specific task, strongly suggests that the operators have an internal framework that automates the compilation and packaging of commands," ESET researcher Matías Porolli said. "Combined with a codebase built around modular, interchangeable components, the impression is one of a mature, well-engineered platform – rather than a loose collection of scripts."

keytmj.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 10, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security Four flaws that attackers could exploit without logging in were fixed today as part of SAP's monthly Security Patch Day—the vendor rates all four 10.0, the maximum CVSS score. Three are in the SAP NetWeaver application server, the software SAP systems run on, and one is in the Web Dispatcher, which receives web requests from the internet and passes them on to that server. The flaws in the Web Dispatcher and the Internet Communication Manager (ICM), which handles the server's web traffic, could allow an attacker who can reach the software over the network to run code, the vendor says. The flaw in the server's SAML 2.0 service provider, which hands off user sign-in to an identity provider, could allow an attacker to log in as any user on some systems that use SAML single sign-on. The flaw in SAP Gateway, which connects the server to other SAP systems and programs, could allow an attacker to impersonate one of the system's own servers and take unauthorized actions. None of the four require any user action to work. Affected Versions and SAP Notes Each flaw is fixed in its own note, and the affected versions differ by component, according to SAP's November security bulletin. The notes are in SAP for Me, which requires a sign-in, and the vendor strongly recommends applying them as a priority. CVE Component SAP Note Affected versions CVE-2026-76964 Internet Communication Manager (ICM), SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP Note 3778530 KRNL64UC 7.53, KERNEL 7.53, 7.54, 7.77, 7.93, 9.16, 9.18, 9.20 CVE-2026-89126 SAP Web Dispatcher Note 3778556 HDB 2.00, KRNL64UC 7.53, WEBDISP 7.53, 7.54, 7.77, 7.93, 9.16, XS_ADVANCED_RUNTIME 1.00, SAP_EXTENDED_APP_SERVICES 1, KERNEL 7.53, 7.54, 7.77, 7.93, 9.16, 9.18, 9.20 CVE-2026-89103 SAP Gateway Note 3798345 KRNL64NUC 7.22, 7.22EXT, KRNL64UC 7.22, 7.22EXT, 7.53, 8.04, KERNEL 7.22, 7.53, 7.54, 7.77, 7.93, 8.04, 9.16, 9.20, 9.21 CVE-2026-120017 SAML2 service provider, SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP and ABAP Platform Note 3849308 SAP_BASIS 702, 731, 740, 750, 751, 752, 753, 754, 755, 756, 757, 758, 816, 920, 921, 922 What Each Flaw Allows On the affected SAML setups, an attacker could use CVE-2026-120017 to log in as privileged users too, according to the vendor. A full compromise could follow, possibly reaching connected systems. A different SAML flaw in the same software, CVE-2026-44748, was fixed on June 9 and needed an attacker with a normal user account. In the ICM flaw (CVE-2026-76964) and the Web Dispatcher flaw (CVE-2026-89126), crafted network traffic could corrupt memory. An attacker who succeeds could then run code and fully compromise the system. SAP Gateway uses access control lists to decide which outside programs may connect to it and which programs it may start. In CVE-2026-89103, the gateway enables its default list with high privileges, allowing an external attacker to be treated as one of the system's own application servers. That attacker could then take unauthorized actions in the application environment. What to Do In its Patch Day analysis, RedRays, a company that reviewed the notes in SAP for Me today, advises updating the kernel and all Web Dispatchers in a single rollout. That rollout should reach levels that cover all 17 of this month's kernel and Web Dispatcher fixes. The firm's guidance for each flaw: SAML2 (CVE-2026-120017). Under certain configurations, the service provider did not check signatures on incoming assertions. Treat any AS ABAP system that uses SAML2 for browser logon, such as Fiori Launchpad or Web GUI behind an identity provider, as in scope until shown otherwise. There is no workaround, so the correction instructions or the listed support package are the only fix. The firm's SAML2 analysis also suggests reviewing every trusted identity provider in transaction SAML2 and checking audit logs for SAML logons by privileged users from unexpected sources. SAP Gateway (CVE-2026-89103). Where secinfo and reginfo hold no explicit rules, or rely on the internal host keyword, the gateway falls back to rules that allow the system's own application servers. An attacker who passes as one of them could then reach the usual gateway attack paths toward command execution. The note lists no workaround. For kernels up to 7.77, the fix adds the profile parameter gw/acl_mode_proxy, which tightens the default rules, while kernels from 7.93 on already have it. The firm's Gateway analysis advises setting it after patching and checking that gw/acl_mode is 1, that secinfo and reginfo hold explicit rules, and that the gateway port (33xx) cannot be reached from user networks or the internet. ICM (CVE-2026-76964). WebSocket control frames with invalid length fields cause a heap out-of-bounds write before any login. SAP NetWeaver AS Java is not affected, and the fix ships through dw.sar and the SP Stack Kernel. If users reach the ICM only through a Web Dispatcher, patching that Web Dispatcher to the levels in FAQ note 3778788 shields the ICM for now, according to the firm's ICM analysis. That holds only if nobody can reach the ICM ports directly. Turning off WebSocket support blocks the bug as a last resort, but it breaks features that depend on it. Web Dispatcher (CVE-2026-89126). It has the same root cause as the ICM flaw. It affects standalone and embedded Web Dispatchers, including those in SAP HANA XS Classic and XS Advanced, but not SAP Content Server. The firm's Web Dispatcher analysis lists the patch paths: SAPWEBDISP.SAR for standalone instances, dw.sar or the SP Stack Kernel for embedded ones, SPS08 revision 089.05 or SPS07 revision 079.11 for HANA XS Classic, and version 1.5.4 or later for XS Advanced. Turning off WebSocket support works until the patch is in, but the note warns that this affects ABAP Push Channels and some Fiori features. Find every Web Dispatcher first, because one missed instance leaves the flaw open.

l5yu54.text: An October cyberattack on refrigeration controllers at about 700 French retail sites was carried out by a cyber unit of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), the French government said yesterday. The attackers broke into controllers on the night of October 11 and changed their defrost settings to high temperatures. That caused food losses and, in at least 15 cases, fires. The unit is called Shahid Kaveh. It is known mainly through hacktivist personas, such as CyberAveng3rs and Cyber Isnaad Front, that publicly claim some of its attacks, France says. France's Foreign Ministry plans to summon Iran's ambassador and to ask its European partners to adopt new sanctions against Iranian organizations and individuals involved in the attack. The Paris prosecutor's office opened a judicial investigation yesterday against the unit's head, the head's two deputies and anyone else identified. It has asked for international arrest warrants. The offenses under investigation include illegally interfering with computer systems and causing damage by means dangerous to people, both made more serious by the aim of serving a foreign power, Iran. In the October attack, the attackers took remote control of Danfoss and Dixell refrigeration controllers through web interfaces, the prosecutor's office said in a press release. They started abnormal defrost cycles with no time limit and switched off the temperature probes' safety alerts, which should go off above a certain temperature. The attack caused about 20 fires. Most of the organizations hit were large retailers, according to a joint report by France's cyber crisis coordination center, known as C4. They include Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour and Intermarché. Small butcher shops, a slaughterhouse and cooperative food plants were also among the victims. The center also tied the attack to the simultaneous targeting of Schneider Electric equipment at several small hydroelectric installations in France. The effects on that equipment were moderate. In its attribution statement, the ministry estimated the food losses at several tens of millions of euros and called the operation the first offensive cyber campaign on French soil carried out purely for sabotage. How France Tied the Attack to Iran The C4 brings together France's national cybersecurity agency (ANSSI), the DGSE and DGSI security services, the armament directorate and the cyber defense command. It says four indicators point to the IRGC as the sponsor of the attack and to Shahid Kaveh as the unit that carried it out. The infrastructure used in the attack was also used during the same period for reconnaissance of Schneider Electric equipment. That equipment is installed at sites such as small- and medium-sized energy and water production sites. The reconnaissance relied on techniques that Shahid Kaveh has used since at least April. The attackers also used FOFA, a scanning tool they usually use. CyberbanNews, a propaganda outlet linked to the unit, reported on the attack as early as October 13. The attack infrastructure also held traces of Persian. Prosecutors said the criminal investigation, run by France's anti-cybercrime office (OFAC) and the DGSI, found an attack method typical of the unit. It also found the use of Persian and IP addresses leading to devices located in Iran. Shahid Kaveh has previously claimed attacks on industrial equipment, according to C4. Through CyberAveng3rs, it claimed an earlier campaign against Unitronics, an Israeli company that makes industrial control systems, in November 2023. In March and April, it claimed a large sabotage campaign against Israeli and U.S. interests that hit industrial control equipment, including Israeli refrigeration equipment. France's attribution does not mention the new wave of refrigeration attacks that struck supermarkets in several other European countries last week. What Operators Should Do France's CERT-FR said in an incident alert that it was aware of numerous compromises affecting remote refrigeration controllers across four product families. They are the Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC series, the Copeland xweb, and the Dixell xweb. The alert, last updated on October 16, warned that attack campaigns against this equipment were probably still underway, and that exposing a management interface to the internet goes against good practice. For controllers that are not compromised, the alert's steps are: Remove internet exposure from these units and from any unit reachable at a public IP address. Check insurance contract terms before cutting off the data feed to the refrigeration contractor. Review the full configuration, especially the defrost ranges. Restore access only through a secure VPN or a protected network. In an emergency, filtering the contractors' IP addresses at a firewall is possible, but it is not a lasting fix. Follow the maker's recommended practices. For Danfoss devices, this includes updating firmware, setting the security level to Strict, and ensuring default passwords have been changed. For compromised controllers, the steps are: Remove internet exposure and check insurance terms, as above. Restart Danfoss equipment, or otherwise restore the device to its factory settings. Restore access only through a secure VPN or a protected network. As above, firewall filtering of contractors' IP addresses is an emergency option, not a lasting fix. Reconfigure the device before putting it back into service, then follow the maker's recommended practices. An end-of-life (EOL) device that receives no security fixes faces a very high risk of compromise if it remains exposed to the internet, the alert warns. In that case, a factory reset alone is not enough: it removes the attackers' persistence, but the device stays vulnerable and will almost certainly be compromised again.

1fa3i4t.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 10, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Application Security Anthropic on Monday released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 models, which it said exhibit improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision. During pre-release training, the large language models (LLMs) helped its engineers "complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours." The artificial intelligence (AI) company said high-stakes risks arising from misalignment remain low, and claimed the models matched or performed better than Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 on most alignment measures, resistance to misuse, honesty, and factuality. "It was roughly an order of magnitude less likely than Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 to publish harmful content to public package registries without encouragement, though it still did so when encouraged by the simulated user," Anthropic noted in its system card. On Irregular's CyScenarioBench, which measures whether a model can plan and execute a multi-stage cyber operation in a realistic environment, Fable 5.2 completed 76.3% of all challenges, compared to 61.7% for Fable 5.1 and 61% for OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber. In a pair of reports published over the last month, Irregular said Google's Gemini 4 Argon solved 12 challenges in the subset of the CyScenarioBench suite end to end, up from 5 for Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber and none for Gemini 3.1 Pro. "On CyScenarioBench, GPT-6 Cyber completed 11 of 11 long-horizon scenarios at least once, compared with 8 of 11 for GPT-6 Astra. Its average success rate was 61%, an increase of 7 percentage points," the AI testing lab said. "On Atomic Challenges, GPT-6 Cyber solved all 22 challenges. Average success rates were 97% in vulnerability research and exploitation, 98% in network attack simulation, and 63% in evasion." Fable 5.2 also scored 89.6% on the CVE Rediscovery benchmark, Anthropic's own internal evaluation of whether an AI model can independently rediscover known vulnerabilities given only the affected source code. The assessment includes 1,829 advisories for open-source projects published in October 2026. Describing Claude Mythos 5.2 as its "most capable model for cybersecurity engineering," Anthropic said it can flag more vulnerabilities than prior models, while simultaneously getting better at reproducing and fixing them. As before, the model's cyber capabilities are accessible through its Cyber Verification Program. Claude Fable 5.2 is available on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. The development comes as Anthropic updated Claude Security with continuous code scanning and automatic fix tracking to help security teams monitor and address vulnerabilities as code changes. "Each finding comes with a severity rating, judged against your project's threat model, and an explanation of how an attacker could reach the vulnerable code, so teams can fix what's actually reachable first," Anthropic said.

oj5ea3.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 10, 2026Vulnerability / Browser Security Google on Monday released updates to patch nine security vulnerabilities, including one that has come under active exploitation in the wild. The high-severity vulnerability, assigned the CVE identifier CVE-2026-125350 (CVSS score: N/A), has been described as a use-after-free bug in the XML component. Use-after-free bugs typically occur when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has already been freed. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to achieve data corruption, program crashes, or arbitrary code execution. An anonymous security researcher has been credited with discovering and reporting the flaw on November 6, 2026. Google acknowledged it is "aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," but has not revealed any additional specific information related to how it's being abused in real-world attacks or who is behind them. "Access to bug details and links may be kept restricted until a majority of users are updated with a fix," the tech giant added. "We will also retain restrictions if the bug exists in a third-party library that other projects similarly depend on, but haven't yet fixed." With the latest development, Google has addressed a total of eight actively exploited Chrome zero-days since the start of the year. This includes CVE-2026-2441, CVE-2026-3909, CVE-2026-3910, CVE-2026-5281, CVE-2026-11645, CVE-2026-85046, and CVE-2026-87491. For optimal protection, users are advised to update their Chrome browser to versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Apple macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. To ensure the latest updates are installed, users can navigate to More > Help > About Google Chrome and select Relaunch. Users of other Chromium-based browsers, such as Microsoft Edge, Brave, Opera, and Vivaldi, are also advised to apply the fixes as and when they become available.

kqrepa.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 10, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security N-able said it has taken N-central Hosted Environments offline and is urging on-premises customers to shut down their servers until further notice following the public disclosure of over 30 vulnerabilities collectively tracked as Able2Shell. "As a precautionary measure, we are temporarily taking our Hosted N-central environment offline while we take the necessary actions to secure the environment and implement appropriate remediation," N-able said. "During this time, customers will be unable to access their Hosted N-central classic environment, and associated services may be unavailable. However, the Ecoverse services under N-able Login remain available and online, including Asset View, Patching, Vulnerability Management, scripting, policies and tagging." The company also said it has not observed any signs of active exploitation of these vulnerabilities, adding it's currently working on a hot fix to address them. The following services are impacted - N-central (hosted version) (Americas) N-central (hosted version) (APAC) N-central (hosted version) (Europe) N-central On-premise (Americas) N-central On-premise (APAC) N-central On-premise (Europe) The development comes as independent security researcher Sean Bales disclosed multiple security flaws along with proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits. The researcher said the issues were tested against N-able N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31. The identified zero-day vulnerabilities include credential disclosure, arbitrary file writes, directory traversal, cross-site scripting (XSS), XML external entity (XXE) injection, and remote code execution (RCE) flaws - Multiple N-central zero-days enable anonymous credential theft, administrator creation, and nable/root RCE. Chains include XXE/NCI trust abuse, support-token theft, unsigned NSP execution, XSS-to-OGNL, and authenticated reverse shells. Arbitrary file writes, traversal, credential disclosure, MDM impersonation, audit tampering, and privileged-helper injection. A native GenericTCP stack overflow also achieves root command execution Successful exploitation of these flaws can allow rogue administrative access to the N-central management interface and facilitate command execution as root. Update watchTowr, in a post shared on X, said it "observed exploitation attempts against N-able N-central honeypots overnight following the 'Able2Shell' zero-days being dropped." The preemptive exposure management firm is urging users to audit for signs of compromise, restrict access, and follow vendor guidance on mitigation steps.

tiwutz.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 10, 2026Vulnerability / Cyber Attack The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Monday added four security flaws impacting GPUStack, SignalWire FreeSwitch, OpenBSD OpenSSH, and IBM Aspera Faspex to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation. The vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-123218 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An incorrect authorization vulnerability in IBM Aspera Faspex that could allow an authenticated user to craft a specific message to bypass authorization, causing privilege escalations. (Fixed in November 2026) CVE-2026-116779 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A code injection vulnerability in SignalWire FreeSwitch that could result in configuration and credential disclosure, arbitrary call control, and command execution. (Fixed in October 2026) CVE-2026-123158 aka SSHole (CVSS score: 8.1) - An unexpected status code or return value vulnerability in OpenBSD OpenSSH on Linux that could allow for authentication bypass. (Fixed in November 2026) CVE-2026-102895 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An improper authentication vulnerability in GPUStack that could allow improper authentication vulnerability which could allow unauthenticated administrative access, including user and model changes, persistent administrator API-key creation, disclosure of worker and cloud-provider secrets, and code execution through POST /v2/inference-backends/from-yaml. (Fixed in July 2026) The addition of CVE-2026-123158 to the KEV catalog follows reports of exploitation attempts targeting the flaw since November 6, 2026. A total of 22 exploitation attempts have been recorded from 14 unique IP addresses so far, according to Previdian. In a post shared on X on November 7, 2026, Defused Cyber said it "observed a small amount of actors targeting SSHole" but stressed the exploitation activity is not widespread yet. According to GreyNoise, the first exploitation attempt against its honeypot network was observed on November 7, 2026, at 12:46 a.m. UTC. Confirmed post-exploitation activity has been detected from six source IP addresses, representing 18 distinct attack chains to date. These involve reconnaissance, queries to cloud metadata services, attempts to read password hashes and root SSH keys, and efforts to modify the SSH authorized_keys file to gain persistent access. In at least one case, an unknown threat actor dubbed GT10 has been observed deploying TAC Agent, a Python-based command-and-control (C2) agent capable of shell command execution, system reconnaissance, directory enumeration, file transfer, and updating itself. Threat intelligence firm watchTowr said it has also observed the OpenSSH flaw being weaponized in the wild for botnet and cryptocurrency miner activity. In an advisory for CVE-2026-102895 published on July 31, 2026, the maintainers of the GPUStack Python package credited Nikko Enggaliano, Wei Yunzhou, Rui Yang, and Haoyu Wang for independently reporting the flaw, adding that "active in-the-wild exploitation" was reported by Ulex Innovative Systems' Javier Sixto. There are currently no public reports on how the other vulnerabilities are being exploited, who is behind them, and the scale of such efforts. Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the fixes by November 12, 2026.

1cmpi0g.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 09, 2026Cloud Security / Data Breach An attacker broke into AWS accounts belonging to multiple Qubole customers between October 14 and October 26 and stole stored secrets and data, cloud security company Wiz said today. The attacker used credentials for an AWS account that Qubole's platform uses to reach those customers. How the attacker got those credentials has not been disclosed. Qubole, a data lake platform owned by Idera, operates within its customers' AWS accounts. To let it in, a customer creates an IAM role, which is an AWS identity with its own set of permissions. The role's trust policy allows Qubole's AWS account to assume the role, granting those permissions. Each request to do this, called AssumeRole, must include a matching code from Qubole known as an External ID. Apart from the attack, most of the roles the attacker assumed were unused, according to Wiz's researchers. But each role still trusted Qubole's account, so the attacker's requests worked. Any organization that has connected Qubole to AWS, even one that no longer uses it, should check its CloudTrail logs from October 1 onward. The sign to look for is an AssumeRole request from the account Qubole's platform uses, 805246085872, that came from an address outside AWS. The researchers did not say whether the credentials have since been disabled or whether the activity has stopped. Neither Qubole nor Idera had posted a statement about the attack on their websites when The Hacker News checked today. Why the Roles Let the Attacker In Every AssumeRole request tied to the attacker carried an External ID and was accepted, the researchers said in their technical analysis. AWS accepts an AssumeRole request for such a role when it comes from the trusted account and includes the correct External ID. The code is not treated as a secret, and anyone with access to the role can view it, according to AWS's external ID guidance. Sentra spotted the activity in several of its customers' environments and alerted the researchers. In the accounts the researchers examined, the attacker looked for stored credentials. It read environment variables for Lambda functions, pulled secrets from Secrets Manager, and read values from the SSM Parameter Store. It then ran the credentials it had found through TruffleHog to test whether they worked. These were the victims' own AWS access keys, Entra ID client secrets, and Okta client credentials. The attacker also copied data out of S3. It retrieved data from any bucket a role could access rather than searching for specific data, and sometimes downloaded an entire bucket in a single session. The researchers have not linked this campaign to any other publicly reported activity, and say the targeting does not match what state-backed groups usually go after. Qubole also lets customers connect with AWS access keys instead of a role. From October 8 to October 11, an attacker used customers' own AWS access keys, which the researchers believe had been set up for Qubole. That attacker then compromised a few of the victims' cloud environments. This activity has not been linked to the AssumeRole abuse. How to Check Your Accounts Wiz's hunting guidance covers CloudTrail logs from October 1 onward in every AWS account that holds a Qubole role. Look for: Account: AssumeRole requests where userIdentity.accountId is 805246085872 and sourceIPAddress is not an AWS address. The researchers saw Qubole's real traffic come only from AWS. IAM principal ID: AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS. Any activity from this IAM user should be investigated, because only the attacker used it in the accounts the researchers examined. IAM principal ID: AIDAJYRRH5Y3A7AAJM2HW, when the source address is outside AWS. The attacker used this IAM user from October 18, but Qubole's normal traffic also uses it. IP: 57.129.54[.]120 and 2001:41d0:70d[:]7800::, OVH-hosted addresses that the attacker used. IP: 45.83.220[.]211, 185.209.199[.]73 and 89.37.63[.]175, which are Mullvad VPN addresses. Other VPN users share them, so a match alone is not proof. Session name: role sessions that start with quiam-, such as quiam-enum. User agent: TruffleHog on GetCallerIdentity calls from one of the IP addresses above. Look for the same user agent in your identity provider's sign-in logs. For every suspicious session, review everything it did afterward, especially in Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, Lambda, and S3. CloudTrail management events log each AssumeRole request and bucket listing, but not which S3 objects were read. That needs S3 data events or S3 server access logs. Several victims lacked the required logs, so responders could not determine which objects the attacker had read. How to Close the Route The researchers recommend these steps: If the attacker assumed one of your Qubole roles, rotate all secrets, parameters, and Lambda environment variables that role had access to, and revoke the role's active sessions. Rotating a credential does not end sessions that were already issued. Remove any Qubole role you no longer need, or take Qubole's account out of its trust policy. Where Qubole supports it, swap the account-wide :root principal in the trust policy for the specific IAM principal that Qubole uses. Add an aws:SourceIp or aws:SourceVpce condition that limits AssumeRole requests to the vendor's documented network ranges. In this attack, the researchers said, "a source IP condition alone would have blocked every role assumption we observed." Assume others can see the External ID. It is logged in plain text in CloudTrail, and vendors and infrastructure-as-code files often store it, so do not use it as your only control. After an incident like this, change it to Qubole and use a different value for each role where possible. Review what each vendor role can reach. Qubole's setup guide includes a sample S3 policy that lets the role read every bucket in the account. Vendor roles are often granted access to Lambda settings, Secrets Manager, SSM parameters, and broad S3 read permissions for convenience, according to the researchers. Set alerts for AssumeRole requests from a vendor account that arrive through a VPN or a hosting company the vendor has not used before. Log every account and region with an organization trail, and enable S3 data events or server access logs for buckets that store sensitive data.

15lo983.text: Attackers used the Ethersphere project's own release automation to publish malicious versions of two of its tools for the Swarm decentralized storage network: bee-js 13.3.0 and Swarm Desktop 0.56.2. Both releases download and run code built to steal the wallet key that Swarm Desktop keeps for its node, along with the stored password that unlocks it. The code is also built to install a backdoor on Windows, macOS, and Linux machines. The bee-js package is the JavaScript library behind Swarm Desktop and the swarm-cli command-line tool. Swarm Desktop runs a Swarm node on a user's own computer and saves the node's private keys there. Both malicious releases have been taken down, and the project's maintainers released a clean Swarm Desktop update today. Neither step removes a backdoor already installed nor protects a key already sent. No theft of funds had been reported at the time of writing. Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 appeared on GitHub at about 00:36 UTC today and was withdrawn about 8.5 hours later. The app's built-in updater could offer it to Windows x64 computers and Apple Silicon Macs within about 10 minutes, according to an incident analysis by Socket, a supply chain security firm. Intel Macs were never offered it, and Linux installs do not update automatically. The bee-js release, version 13.3.0, was the latest version on npm for about 75 minutes, from 00:09 to 01:25 UTC today. Its code runs as a postinstall script, which npm executes automatically during installation unless install scripts are disabled. A project did not need to import the library for the code to run. The project's own swarm-cli and bee-dashboard packages, and the Swarm Desktop source code, accepted version ranges that included 13.3.0. A fresh install within that window could have pulled in the malicious version. None of the reports gave a count of infected machines. The firm's rough estimate is that bee-js 13.3.0 was downloaded about 10 times, including by security scanners and mirrors. Swarm Desktop 0.56.2's download count reached 65 by 08:27 UTC, including researchers. Ethersphere's maintainers withdrew 0.56.2 and replaced it today with a clean release, version 0.56.3. In the change that set up the new release, one of them wrote that 0.56.2 "was published by an attacker using stolen CI credentials and has been withdrawn." Version 0.56.3 is the same code as the previous version, 0.56.1, signed with a newly issued Developer ID certificate, according to that maintainer's incident note. The note says the app's auto-updater will move installs of 0.56.2 to it, although Linux packages still need to be replaced by hand. A comparison of the two versions' source code by The Hacker News found no changes beyond the version number and release notes. When The Hacker News checked npm today, 13.2.0 was again the latest bee-js version, and 13.3.0 could no longer be downloaded from the registry. What to Do The GitHub advisory for bee-js 13.3.0 says: "Any computer that has this package installed or running should be considered fully compromised." SafeDep, a software supply chain security company, offers the same advice for any computer on which Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 was installed. If you use bee-js in a project or CI job: Search lockfiles, package caches, internal registries, and CI install logs for @ethersphere/bee-js@13.3.0, including copies pulled in by other packages. Pin 13.2.0, and clear cached copies of 13.3.0, including any npm mirror you install through. If 13.3.0 was installed with install scripts turned on, treat that machine or CI runner as compromised, even if the install log shows no errors. The code hides its own network errors. From a clean computer, rotate every password, token, and key that the installing user or CI job could read. If you run Swarm Desktop: Look for the line Bee Desktop version: 0.56.2 (production) in the app's log file, bee-desktop.log. Version 0.56.2 is written at every launch, just before the malicious code runs. The log folder is ~/Library/Logs/Swarm Desktop/ on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA%\Swarm Desktop\Log\ on Windows, and ~/.local/state/Swarm Desktop/ on Linux. Install 0.56.3. On Linux, replace the package by hand. If 0.56.2 ever ran, treat the node's key and password as stolen. From a clean computer, move the node's funds, chequebook, and stake to a new key. On any machine where the code ran: Remove the ~/.solidity/ folder, the solidity-langsupport-runner.service user service on Linux, the com.solidity.langsupport.runner LaunchAgent on macOS, and the ScreenConnect Client (5cbe79c9c25524df) service on Windows. Updating, reinstalling, or removing the app or package does not remove them. Where possible, rebuild the machine from a trusted image instead of cleaning it in place. How the Malware Works Both releases carry the same loader, SafeDep found in its technical analysis. It is a few lines of code that download more code from api.frameworkmetrics[.]xyz and run it with the user's permissions. In bee-js the loader is the postinstall script, and in Swarm Desktop it runs each time the app starts. The downloaded code looks for two files in Swarm Desktop's data folder: config.yaml and data-dir/keys/swarm.key. If both are there, it sends them to the attackers' server. The key file is an encrypted Ethereum keystore, but Swarm Desktop keeps its password in plain text in config.yaml. With both files, the attackers can take the node wallet's xDAI and xBZZ tokens, its chequebook funds, and its stake, the company says. The downloaded code also installs a backdoor. On Linux and macOS, it is a Go remote shell called evjawbreaker, saved in a hidden ~/.solidity folder. It runs in the background as a user service on Linux and as a LaunchAgent on macOS. The shell reads the address of its control server from an Ethereum smart contract, so the attackers can change that address at any time. They had updated it 29 minutes before the malicious bee-js code was added. On Windows, the downloaded code installs a genuine ScreenConnect remote-access client, signed by its maker, ConnectWise. The client runs as a system service and connects to the attackers' relay. If the user is an administrator, the code gets administrator rights through a known way around the User Account Control prompt. If not, it shows the prompt again whenever the user cancels. With those rights, it adds a Microsoft Defender exclusion and installs the client silently. How the Releases Got Out Both releases came from bee-worker, the account Ethersphere uses to automate its releases. Neither change was signed nor submitted as a pull request. For bee-js, the attackers published a GitHub release for the new version, which started the project's npm publishing workflow. That workflow needed no approval and published the package to npm in 73 seconds, according to Socket. Because the project's real workflow built it, the package carried valid provenance, the record that links an npm package to the repository and workflow that built it. Provenance shows where a package was built, not whether anyone reviewed the code inside it. For Swarm Desktop, the attackers manually started a build workflow that had the project's Apple and Windows signing certificates and needed no approval. The macOS app was signed with the project's Developer ID and notarized by Apple, so macOS displayed only its normal first-launch prompt, the firm found. The maintainers have since made the app's signing jobs wait for approval from the project's DevOps team and run only from the main branch. How the attackers gained access remained unclear at the time of writing. The maintainer's incident note blames the theft of CI credentials and secrets. The firm's analysis indicates that two GitHub accounts were used: bee-worker and a long-time maintainer's account. None of the reports explained how the credentials were stolen. Links to Earlier Attacks The payloads share an Ethereum contract, a ScreenConnect relay, and file names with fake extensions for Solidity developers that appeared on the Open VSX marketplace in September. Researchers at Pluto Security described those extensions in their October 1 EtherDuck analysis. Pluto ties them "with high confidence" to the group behind the original SleepyDuck extension, which read its server address from a different Ethereum contract in 2025. Socket says the same group is behind the bee-js and Swarm Desktop releases. Indicators of Compromise Defenders can search logs and machines for the following. Domain: api.frameworkmetrics[.]xyz URL path: /v1/analytics (bee-js loader) URL path: /v1/electron (Swarm Desktop loader) URL path: /v1/assets/ (further payloads) URL path: /v1/swarm/report (stolen wallet files) HTTP header: X-Ethersphere: 1 IP:port: 193[.]57[.]9[.]155:4912 (evjawbreaker control server) IP:port: 185[.]232[.]84[.]169:8041 (ScreenConnect relay) Ethereum contract: 0xf8a900Db50b3331be6B768bA460BB59f3E40C344 Path: ~/.solidity/ systemd unit: solidity-langsupport-runner.service LaunchAgent: com.solidity.langsupport.runner Service: ScreenConnect Client (5cbe79c9c25524df) SHA-256: 9b73e7cd4e1425e770392549d8df46c706139ef476f4f7b9ac405165dc8d9696 (linux_amd64) SHA-256: b601776817363b96295119f7221338a122d5247a35a77a64b04f286e1bbcc565 (linux_arm64) SHA-256: 80d2672e2599732d3c0ae2a4cd0d1e3fe4d555a60273ce33feb99db3f34d250f (darwin_amd64) SHA-256: fae61f31f00988fdc5cc9e7272b51e08af2e245d81003237875415930fd27358 (darwin_arm64) SHA-256: 37d14bff30762ca701e9c1f8bc6c57c065bb20ae3a2208cb7411a6530610f08e (invoke.ps1) SHA-256: 7527e86d70e7c9493db4356f1c3775380431b310000f2602c1e993cf435d01da (app.msi)

1od6fs3.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 09, 2026Cyber Espionage / Threat Intelligence The South Asian cyber espionage group known as Bitter (aka APT-C-08, APT-Q-37, Hazy Tiger, Orange Yali, T-APT-17, and TA397) has been observed targeting South Asian organizations with a previously unreported remote access trojan called PapRAT. "PapRAT has both C++ and Rust implementations," Fortinet FortiGuard Labs researcher Cara Lin said. "Its capabilities include command execution, file uploads and downloads, file deletion, directory and drive enumeration, and screenshot capture. The Rust variant adds PowerShell execution and other commands." The campaign is notable for making use of three different infection chains - A Windows Shortcut (LNK) file that abuses the native "ftp.exe" utility to run scripts and create scheduled tasks designed to maintain contact with a command-and-control (C2) server. A VHDX disk image containing a LNK file that launches a lure Microsoft Excel spreadsheet, while running an MSI installer in the background to deploy PapRAT. A URL shortcut (URL) file that fetches a LNK file via WebDAV, which then leads to an MSI installer that deploys PapRAT. The living-off-the-land (LotL) approach is designed to execute commands from a remote server ("goodnfortunes[.]com"), allowing it to collect directory and task lists, directory information from Desktop, Documents, and Downloads, installed antivirus product data, and mounted drives. The harvested reconnaissance information is saved as "abc.pdf" and exfiltrated back to the C2 server via a curl command, after which the staged file is deleted from the host. A second version of the script has been found to retrieve a file called "talk.log" from "techtalkhelp[.]com." The payload contains a Base64-encoded script to obtain additional instructions from the same server and execute them as PowerShell commands. "This staging model gives the attacker operational flexibility, while the commands are updated server-side without pushing a new binary, avoiding PE drops and process injection that some security appliances could easily detect," Fortinet said. The PapRAT malware delivered via the MSI installer in the second attack chain is designed for remote control. It supports eight commands - MSG, for remote shell FDD, for directory listing DEL, for file deletion RUN, for arbitrary file execution GDR, for drive enumeration SS1, for screenshot capture UPP, for uploading local files to the C2 server ("rivingtonclarks[.]com") DWW, for downloading files from the C2 server A Rust version of the malware incorporates three more commands - MS2, for PowerShell command execution SLP, for sleeping and polling resumption BYE, for process termination A notable aspect of the third attack chain is that it combines the salient aspects of the first two sequences by using a script to download an MSI installer via curl. Like before, the MSI installer serves as a conduit for PapRAT, which then proceeds to drop WmRAT, a malware previously identified as used by Bitter. The findings indicate that the threat actor continues to refine its custom arsenal to establish and maintain access to targeted systems. "These changes underscore the importance of monitoring malicious behavior across scripting tools, scheduled tasks, and installer activity alongside detecting known malware signatures," Fortinet said. "Organizations should treat unexpected LNK files, URL shortcuts, disk images, and MSI packages with caution, particularly when delivered through unsolicited messages."

eg22o7.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 09, 2026Cybersecurity News / Hacking A system doesn't always need a complicated bug to let someone in. Sometimes, a blank password is enough. That's one of the bigger stories this week. And it gets worse when the tools meant to keep systems updated or running safely become part of the attack. Elsewhere, attackers are hiding inside normal web traffic, stealing credentials from network devices, and finding new uses for exposed systems. AI is helping some of them move faster, but old mistakes are doing plenty of the work too. Even forgotten settings and small changes made months ago are coming back to cause trouble. There's a lot packed into this week's news, including some strange research findings, fresh attacks, and a few warnings worth taking seriously. Here's the full recap. ⚡ Threat of the Week OpenSSH Flaw Sees Exploitation Attempts — Threat actors are attempting to exploit a recently disclosed security flaw impacting OpenSSH that can enable sign-ins to accounts that have no password set. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS score: 8.1) and codenamed SSHole (or *sshole), impacts Linux systems that run OpenSSH on the musl C library with Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) disabled, including Alpine Linux's default OpenSSH server configuration. As of November 9, 2026, a total of 20 exploitation attempts have been recorded from 13 unique IP addresses from Denmark, Iran, Japan, the Netherlands, Norway, Singapore, Sweden, Switzerland, and the U.S. 🔔 Top News Trojanized CWP Web Server Used to Deliver CWPdoor — A new Linux malware called CWPdoor is being distributed via a trojanized version of cwpsrv, the built-in daemon and web server that powers the Control Web Panel. According to XLab, a shell script named "cwpsrv_update.sh" is used to download "cwpsrv" from a remote server ("136.0.141[.]71") and replace the legitimate file on the system. "The downloaded cwpsrv is a passive backdoor that can be triggered by specific headers in HTTP/HTTPS traffic to remotely execute commands specified by the attacker," XLab said. "Its backdoor logic is triggered only when it receives a specially crafted request from the attacker. At the same time, it suppresses logging for that request, leaving no trace of the interaction in the access logs. This combination of directly replacing the legitimate cwpsrv binary, passive triggering, and log suppression makes CWPdoor exceptionally stealthy." Debian and Ubuntu APT Flaw Allows Code Execution as Root — A vulnerability in the APT package manager (CVE-2026-109518, CVSS score: 7.7) can be exploited to install a package under certain conditions and achieve code execution with elevated privileges. The issue affects Ubuntu and Debian operating systems. "Under specific conditions, when APT is configured to use HTTP package sources with retry settings enabled, a third-party with a network position between the host and the package mirror can cause APT to install a package that did not pass verification," Amazon said in an advisory. Calling it a "significant escalation" in attacks, the threat actor is said to be re-targeting entities that were originally targeted last month after incomplete remediation, adding that the intrusions "have been timed to coincide with holidays, weekends and other low-monitoring windows to delay detection and response." The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-107441 (CVSS score: 8.8), is an out-of-bounds write flaw that could "allow a LAN-based, unauthenticated attacker to exploit the flaw and potentially execute OS commands via a crafted HTTP request." The activity has been attributed to a Chinese-speaking threat actor tracked as Kapibala (aka Red Heron). The attacker has been found to weaponize the flaw to deploy the JITTERLY backdoor and SIXZUT, a ring 3 rootkit. cPGuard Update Mechanism Hijacked to Deliver Backdoor — Unknown threat actors compromised the update infrastructure for the cPGuard web security suite to distribute a backdoor and a data-stealing script. "On 2 November 2026 at 02:06 UTC, an unidentified attacker used compromised credentials to gain unauthorized access to OPSSHIELD's update distribution infrastructure (CDN)," OPSSHIELD said. "The attacker used this access to distribute a malicious script through the cPGuard update channel." "mSeven Software ('mSeven') recently learned of suspicious activity associated with the mSecure password management application," the company said. The lack of specifics has understandably riled up customers, with one user on Reddit stating "their silence on this is mind-bending." In December 2025, Germany's cyber agency BSI found that mSecure's maker could, in theory, access the data users store in it. ‎️‍🔥 Trending CVEs Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. 1m3snh.text: The login systems behind two car brands' mobile apps could be taken over completely, two security researchers found, allowing them to access any customer's account and, for an owner with a connected car, unlock the doors and start the engine. Both apps signed customers in through ForgeRock, an identity platform now part of Ping Identity, and on those servers the researchers reached an administrator console that still used its default password. They tested the full attack only on their own and consenting owners' cars in the United States, in February 2026, and both systems were fixed about two hours after they reported the problem. Shubham Shah and Sam Curry published their work late last week. They had started with the apps: both brands signed customers in through the same platform, which runs in two parts: one for login and one, called OpenIDM, that holds customer records. OpenIDM comes with a built-in administrator console powered by the Apache Felix tool. ForgeRock's own hardening guide tells operators to remove this console or protect it before going live because it stores its own password separately from the rest of the system. On these servers, it was still there and still used the documented default: the word admin for both the username and the password. The console was blocked from the open internet, but the edge that guards the site and the Java software behind it read the same web address differently. By adding encoded slashes and extra characters, the researchers made the edge treat the request as a harmless static file while the server treated it as the path to the console, and the default password did the rest. The full method is in their technical analysis. Inside the console, the researchers used a built-in scheduler to run small scripts that execute their own code on the identity server. That gave them a command prompt on the machine that holds the customer records for both brands' logins. The records sat behind the same block as the console, but the researchers' code reached them from inside the server. They changed a target account's email address and password, signed in as that customer through the normal app, and received the same access tokens the real app uses. Those tokens were the keys to the car. Using the account's own vehicle commands, the researchers unlocked the doors and started the engine of a test car, with the owner standing next to it, then stopped the engine and locked it again. The researchers were careful about what they had shown. They reported being able to open a session for any customer account on the affected servers, but they ran the vehicle commands only on cars they owned or were allowed to use. They said they "tested the complete chain only with US accounts and vehicles." Shubham Shah published a second attack on the Australian systems behind the same brands. There, the way in was different: admin credentials for the identity server had been left in the app's code, intended for a test setup. He set out the full Australia chain in a separate post. With both attacks together, the researchers said, they could send unlock and engine-start commands to the brands' cars in Australia, the United States, and Canada. That second post does not give a date for when the Australian systems were fixed. The attack left little for an owner to notice. Changing the email and password did not log the owner out of their app, and the researchers could direct the account's alerts to their own phone, keeping them off the owner's phone. The researchers put the real email address back after the test. Neither write-up says whether anyone else found or used the path before it was closed. What Identity Teams Should Check The brands' mistake was in how they ran ForgeRock, not a new bug in the product, so there is no CVE, the public ID that tracks a flaw, and no vendor advisory to follow. The console and its default password have been documented for years, and the maker's production hardening guide already tells operators to remove the console or change its password before going live. For teams running the same identity software, now sold as PingIDM, two checks matter: Look for the Apache Felix console at /system/console, and remove it or change its default password. Do not count on edge or WAF path rules to hide an admin page. A path the edge and the server read differently can slip past the rules, as it did here. The two researchers have a long record of this kind of work, usually breaking into the web systems behind the apps rather than the cars themselves. They have shown remote access to vehicles from Honda, Kia, and Subaru, among others. A Subaru flaw they reported exposed owners' accounts and their cars through that carmaker's connected-car service, and a broader 16-brand study in 2023 found the same kind of web weakness across much of the industry.

1rwjmfv.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 09, 2026Cryptocurrency / Vulnerability Some people who set up a Keplr crypto wallet with their Google or Apple account have had money stolen by an attacker. Keplr uses a company called Web3Auth to run that Google and Apple sign-in. The attacker used a security flaw at that company to reach the wallets, both companies said late last week. Web3Auth then used the attacker's own route to empty other at-risk wallets before the attacker got to them, it said. It moved that money, with help from the wallet maker, into recovery wallets for safekeeping. So an empty balance may mean the money was rescued, not stolen. Wallets made with a recovery phrase (a backup list of 12 or 24 words) or a hardware wallet are not affected, the wallet maker said. It has paused Google and Apple sign-in while it investigates. What Affected Users Should Do The wallet maker has given this user guidance for accounts created with Google or Apple login: Do not send new funds to the account. Do not re-import the account or recreate it anywhere. Move any funds that are not staked or locked to an account that uses a recovery phrase or a hardware wallet. Trust updates only from the official accounts of the wallet maker and the login provider, and ignore direct messages or links that offer "recovery." Staked and locked assets are taking longer to secure. The wallet maker is also working with the login provider on a way for users to check whether their account was affected. In the meantime, the login provider has published a recovery address list, which it says lets people tell its own transfers apart from possibly malicious ones. It has also warned users not to assume that an unfamiliar destination address is linked to the attacker. What Went Wrong In an incident update, Web3Auth said a security issue in its own infrastructure affected certain wallets it provides inside the Keplr app. Keplr went further, saying the flaw led to a "private key breach" for some users who signed in with Google or Apple. A private key is the secret code that approves payments from a wallet, so whoever holds it can move the money. Neither company has said how the flaw worked, when the attacker first used it, or whether that route is now closed. Where the Money Went No dollar figure for the theft has come from either company. Josh Lee, a Keplr co-founder, gave an early estimate in his initial findings: about 20% of Google and Apple login accounts were affected, and only a fraction of those appeared to have been exploited. GoPlus, a Web3 security company, said in a security alert that at least about $1 million had been stolen. It did not explain how it reached that figure. The rescued money went into what the login provider calls secure recovery wallets, on 11 blockchains in the Cosmos family and eight Ethereum-style chains. Bitquery, a blockchain data firm, counted at least $6.01 million moving from more than 44,000 wallets into the recovery wallets by late last week. The firm first reported the transfers as theft. It has since issued a corrected analysis that treats them as the rescue, though it says it cannot check who controls the recovery wallets. The first of these transfers came 21 minutes before the login provider's first public notice, the firm's data shows. Most of the wallets, 86%, were emptied after the wallet maker warned users. The moved funds are safe, the login provider said in its recovery thread, and it is working with the wallet maker to return them to users. It has not said how or when. Beyond Keplr The login provider said the issue affects its services used by some other companies, but Keplr is the only one it has named. It paused its embedded wallet service, which other apps use to build wallets for their users. Its status page still shows its login service as down today. Consensys, the company behind the MetaMask wallet, bought the login provider in June 2025. Its acquisition announcement said the deal would let MetaMask users create and recover wallets with social logins. The provider said its initial investigation found "no evidence that MetaMask users are impacted."

vx5igs.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 09, 2026Vulnerability / Cryptocurrency Everyone running LNbits, a free, open-source Bitcoin Lightning wallet system, should shut down their servers now because of a wave of attacks, the project said yesterday. It has several security fixes to release and asked operators to be careful until they are out. One operator said new accounts used an exploit to withdraw 2,285,545 satoshis, about 0.023 bitcoin, from his server before he could stop it. The shutdown notice came about 80 minutes after a first, narrower warning. That warning asked operators to disable Paywall, an add-on that makes people pay to view content, while the project looked into a possible bug. As of 09:00 UTC today, the project had not released a fixed version. On X, it had not canceled the notice, offered another option, or told operators how to check whether their servers were hit before they were shut down. Ben Arc, an LNbits developer, said in a patch estimate yesterday that patches "should be merged and available within 24-48hrs." Counted from his post, that means between about 14:00 UTC today and 14:00 UTC tomorrow. The project also switched off all the LNbits instances it runs for users on its cloud service, my.lnbits.com, later yesterday. It said in a hosted-service notice that all services would be back within 24 hours, or by about 17:20 UTC today. Kevin Ravensberg, the operator who reported the loss, said in a loss report on X that his server was exploited before the shutdown notice. The attack ran from 09:22 to 14:00 UTC yesterday, starting more than three hours before the project's first warning at 12:33 UTC. He has promised to repay users of BitTipBot, a Telegram bot. They cannot reach their funds until the project fixes the flaws. Later yesterday, Ravensberg said in a follow-up post that Arc and a team of security testers had confirmed "which exact extension exploit was used" on his server. Neither he nor the project had named that extension in posts on X as of 09:00 UTC today. The project also had not said whether it is Paywall, the add-on named in its first warning. The shutdown notice covers LNbits servers and does not mention Lightning nodes or other wallet software. It did not say how many servers were attacked or how much was taken.

uud8z7.text: A single attacker using AI agents pulled emergency dispatch records covering seven Taipei districts, researchers at Acronis's Threat Research Unit said last week. The agents also found a Taipei fire department platform exposing patient data from 2018, including ECG readings and ambulance video footage, without a login. The researchers are highly confident that the attacker is a single person based in Hualien City, Taiwan. He aimed the agents at hundreds of organizations in at least 11 countries, including emergency services, banks, universities and military systems. The agents collected data or accessed systems at about 10 of them in Taiwan, Mexico and Thailand. The evidence comes from the attacker's own server, which initially appeared to be a misconfigured development system. It turned out to be his operational attack platform, containing more than 90,000 files, including the agents' conversations, his command history, hacking tools, credentials, and victims' data. The agents did not communicate with each other, so the attacker manually pasted one agent's output into another. Commercial AI models mostly refused to help him attack. The attacking agents therefore ran almost entirely on "abliterated" models, meaning AI models run locally with their safety training removed. What the Agents Reached Taiwan was targeted far more heavily than any other country, according to the researchers' technical analysis. The most serious confirmed harm there involved emergency-services data. The dispatch records came from a city's system for 119, Taiwan's emergency number for fire and ambulance services. The agents pulled them from the system's API, and they include incident times, response types, case status, and street-level locations. They are case records, not live ambulance tracking. The researchers' summary says breaches at emergency services and universities led to the theft of medical and personal data. Their detailed account of the Taipei patient platform, however, says only that the records were exposed. The agents also went after five other targets tied to Taiwan's emergency services: Target What the agents did Result Fire-dispatch technology vendor Logged into its database admin panel with default root credentials. A web shell attempt through a known CVE failed. Access to 18 or more database tables Emergency management information system Found a hardcoded AES-256 key in the site's front-end JavaScript that exposed session-cookie contents, including an administrator's identity No confirmed compromise National disaster-response center A scanning tool reported a critical Apache remote code execution flaw The flaw did not exist National fire agency single sign-on portal Tried to guess logins (brute force) No confirmed access Fire-department systems in five cities Scanned them to identify the software they run No confirmed compromise The report does not say whether the affected organizations or Taiwan's authorities were told, or whether the exposed data can still be reached. Outside emergency services, the agents pulled data from an account table at a Taiwanese lending firm through SQL injection. In Thailand, they collected data from three universities in the same way, after selecting 489 potential targets across 45 institutions. In Mexico, they collected about 206,800 home phone records containing names and addresses, using government statistics, postal code lists, and telecom authority data. About 15 more organizations were attacked without a confirmed break-in. In at least eight other countries, targets were only scanned or lined up for attacks that had not run by the time the researchers looked. The researchers watched the operation for 12 days. One recorded exchange shows the attacker at work on July 25. How the AI Was Used and Where It Failed The setup, called BOSSAI, had 12 AI agents, with 9 in use. Some built and maintained the attacker's servers and tools, while others scanned targets and carried out attacks. Commercial cloud models did most of the building, with Grok as the main builder. When the attacker directly asked them to attack, Grok and MiniMax M3 refused and requested written proof that the work was authorized. The researchers say it is unclear whether a fake authorization letter would have changed that. Grok made one exception, repairing a broken proof-of-concept script that the attacker then handed to an attack agent. The attacker also redirected the coding agents Claude Code and Codex to an abliterated model, though they mostly did infrastructure work. Cursor, another coding agent, attacked a Taiwanese emergency-services site while running such a model. The abliterated models were versions of DeepSeek, GLM, and Qwen. The agents also got things wrong. One scanning tool invented CVEs, and more than half of its high and critical findings were false positives or wrongly classified. The main attack agent also reported results that had not happened. Who Ran It Acronis's attribution rests on mistakes the attacker made while hiding his identity, combined with publicly available information. He reused a single identity across his legitimate businesses and his attack servers, including a GitHub profile, a logo, an SSH key name, and an email address. His home IP address appeared during an SSH session in one of his Grok conversations. Why he did it is less clear. Some attacks on government, emergency, and military targets looked like the work of state-backed hacking groups, while others looked like ordinary cybercrime. The researchers think he probably wanted to make money, and it is unclear whether he works for anyone. What Stopped the Agents What the agents found was mostly data that was already poorly protected, according to the researchers: a medical data port left open since 2018, dispatch records on a public-facing API, a lender with 16 SQL injection points, and universities running unpatched Oracle databases. The agents failed where logins were enforced, where paywalls required a valid session, and where endpoints were properly filtered. The AI made it cheap to find and reach many targets at once, but it did not get past defenses that held. Nine IP addresses and nine domains from the attacker's setup appear in the indicator list at the end of the analysis. None is marked as active or inactive, and most come without a note on what they were used for.

o506t3.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 09, 2026Cyber Espionage / Insider Threat The OpenAI engineer who was arrested and charged last month for planting a covert audio recording device in the company's office has pleaded not guilty. According to reports from Bloomberg and CNBC, Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan made an appearance in San Francisco federal court on Friday, where he entered the plea. His next hearing is scheduled for November 17, 2026. If proven guilty, the 35-year-old faces a maximum of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by three years of supervised release. He has been held without bail since his arrest on October 9, 2026. Late last month, a grand jury indicted Alfozan on a single count of interception of oral communications. Prosecutors allege that the former OpenAI employee placed a "sophisticated recording device" in an executive OpenAI conference room in what has been described as an attempt to unlawfully record sensitive conversations. He was arrested three days before he, along with his wife and son, were scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way ticket. "His wife and son, however, immediately left the United States without him," U.S. prosecutors said. "Rather than wait until the October 12 flight as booked, they initially planned to fly to Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, on October 11 on a one-way ticket booked and paid for by the Saudi government." "That flight was canceled, however, when a member of the Saudi military booked and paid for yet another one-way ticket for the defendant's wife and son, this one business class to Doha, Qatar, on October 10, 2026. They did make that flight, departing San Francisco about 36 hours after the defendant was arrested." In a subsequent court filing, it was alleged that Alfozan was in frequent contact with a member of the Saudi Royal Family via WhatsApp. He was also deemed a flight risk, with court documents claiming that the defendant took great pains to create bespoke, encrypted recording devices to record sensitive meetings involving senior OpenAI personnel and executives.

18f0h18.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 09, 2026Critical Infrastructure / Cyber Attack U.S. government agencies have warned that threat actors are actively targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems globally with an aim to cause service disruptions, fire hazards, and loss of inventory. "The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards," according to a joint advisory. According to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), Department of Agriculture (USDA), and Department of Transportation (DOT), threat actors are likely to exploit authentication bypasses, arbitrary code injection, and weak configurations to gain access to these systems and cause the following effects - Change of temperature, which, in turn, could affect the service life of the system, create a fire hazard, cause inventory loss, or harm consumers who purchase products after unsafe storage. Loss of visibility into current temperatures due to a denial-of-service. In response to the threat, owners and operators are being urged to use strong authentication, keep systems updated, identify any systems that are accessible from the internet, isolate operational technology (OT) devices, change default passwords, retire and replace legacy devices, remove unnecessary remote access, and secure necessary remote access. "Industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems protect food, medicine, and other temperature-sensitive products, making them attractive targets for malicious cyber actors," said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. "We are seeing these systems targeted across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk." In recent weeks, threat actors have targeted hundreds of supermarkets across Europe by exploiting weaknesses in internet-accessible refrigeration controllers to raise temperatures, in some cases to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit), or force cooling units into defrost mode, spoiling food and resulting in financial losses. Targets of these attacks ranged from major supermarket chains to small grocers and butchers in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Sweden, and the U.K. Among those targeted was the French Blood Establishment, which confirmed that a cybersecurity incident affecting a refrigeration equipment provider had raised temperature and defrost settings to "extremely high levels" at three facilities used to store blood plasma. It's unclear who is behind the hacking spree. Data from Censys shows that there are still hundreds of Danfoss StoreView instances exposed globally, with most of them located in France, although the number has dropped significantly from 3,004 to 708 between October 9 and November 5, 2026. The Copeland/Dixell XWEB exposure, likewise, has declined from 3,708 to 2,420. The attack surface management platform described the refrigeration attacks across Europe as the latest addition to a list of other recent incidents targeting critical infrastructure, including gas station tank gauges, air raid systems, and water towers. "North America accounts for roughly 38% of global ICS [industrial control systems] exposure," Censys said. "Asia's share grew from 22% in 2024 to 25% in 2026, while Europe's fell from 36.5% to 32%. However, these shifts have not produced an overall decline." "While exposure numbers are high, they're hardly surprising: ICS exposure is a problem that's been reported on and warned about for years. It poses a critical risk to the public as gatekeepers to the world's critical infrastructure."
