16bqa46.text: Passwords and API keys that developers typed into commands they approved in Claude Code are sitting in public GitHub repositories, where anyone can read them. When a user selects "Yes, and don't ask again," Anthropic's AI coding assistant can save the command, word-for-word, including the secret, in a project settings file. Software security company Apiiro said yesterday that 1,122 public copies of that file hold at least one secret, though it did not test whether any still work. One company the researchers notified earlier this week confirmed its key had been live. The file is .claude/settings.local.json. Removing it from a project does not undo the leak, because older versions stay in git history and in forks of the repository. The researchers' advice is to rotate first: change every password, token, and key the file has ever held, then clean up. How a Secret Lands in the File By default, Claude Code asks before it runs most shell commands. If the user picks "Yes, and don't ask again," it saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json inside the project, according to its permissions documentation. Matching commands then run without asking in later sessions. The rule covers only what the prompt offered. Sometimes that is a pattern, such as npm test *, and sometimes one exact command. When it is the exact command, any password or token typed into it is saved too, in plain text. In public files, the researchers found saved commands with the secret still inside, and they reproduced the behavior with the latest models, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1. Claude Code tries to keep the file out of git. The first time it writes the file in a git repository, it adds the file to the user's global git excludes, its settings documentation says. Git on that computer then ignores the file in every repository. That protection stays in one user's git settings on one computer. It does nothing for a file that was already committed, the researchers say. Claude Code never adds the file to the project's own .gitignore, so the protection does not travel with the project. In 539 of the 1,105 repositories the researchers traced, a commit listing Claude as a co-author changed the file. They take this to mean Claude often commits the file itself. What Apiiro Found Apiiro's search of public GitHub found 104,185 copies of the file in 103,617 repositories, its research write-up shows. About 1.1% of them, or 1,122 copies, hold at least one secret. Together they hold 1,379 different secrets. A value counted as a secret when it matched a known key format, or when a password or token sat beside the address of a public server. An AI reviewer also had to agree. The researchers do not say whether anyone has used these secrets. More than a third of the secrets open a database directly, including 379 database passwords. Others include 43 SSH logins for public servers, 42 tokens for GitHub, GitLab and npm, and 23 AWS keys. Among the owners of these files are 63 organizations, mostly software companies of all sizes. The strongest cases include a database vendor's own admin-level cloud key and the owner password of a medical-records database, the researchers say. As of Monday, every file with a secret was still on its repository's default branch, and in half of those repositories it had been there for at least 217 days. Older versions of the file contain 734 more secrets across 509 repositories that are not present in any current copy, usually because the file was deleted. Forks spread the files further: 211 forks of 74 repositories carry the same secrets as the originals. Secrets also sit in 298 of 76,011 copies of the shared .claude/settings.json file, which teams commit on purpose, mostly inside allow rules. Including those, the older versions, and saved agent chat logs, the total is 2,539 secrets across 1,994 repositories. Of 16 coding agents whose documentation the researchers compared, Claude Code is the only one confirmed to save the full approved command in a project file by default. What to Do For developers, the researchers recommend these steps: Search your GitHub organization for .claude/settings.local.json and .claude/settings.json, and check each repository's git history for them, even where the files are gone. Rotate every password, token and key the files have ever held, before cleaning up. Stop tracking the local file with git rm --cached .claude/settings.local.json, and add it to the repository's own .gitignore. Open the file on your own computer, even if it was never committed, and delete every rule that contains a secret. Keep secrets out of commands. Refer to them as variables from a secrets manager, such as $DB_URL, so the saved rule holds the variable name and not the secret. Approve patterns, such as Bash(npm run:*), instead of single commands. Copies that never reach GitHub still matter, the researchers say. The file is plain JSON in the project folder, and it can also be left inside an npm package, a Docker image, a zip archive, or a synced folder. Malware has previously looked for secrets on developer machines. In September 2025, the Shai-Hulud worm ran the TruffleHog secret scanner over infected computers, and the scanner flagged more than half of the files as secret. Common secret scanners miss many of these files. The researchers ran gitleaks and TruffleHog over every copy, without the tools' verification step. Of the 1,122 files with a secret, gitleaks flagged 564 and TruffleHog 643, and neither flagged 215. Most misses are passwords typed inside commands. Scanners look for known key formats, and a password after PGPASSWORD=, sshpass -p , or mysql -p looks like an ordinary word in an ordinary command line. For security teams, the researchers recommend: Treat agent folders such as .claude/, .cursor/, .gemini/ and .specstory/, and agent memory files, as holding secrets, like .env files, on laptops as well as in repositories. Add them to pre-commit and CI secret scanning, including git history, and make sure the scanner catches passwords inside commands, not only known key formats. Add .claude/settings.local.json to the organization's .gitignore templates. Check credentials paired with a public server first, because those are the ones that give access. Earlier Reports Claude Code users have reported this behavior before. An earlier bug report, filed on August 11, 2025, said approved commands with API keys and tokens were being stored word for word in settings.local.json. An automated bot closed that report as "not planned" on January 3, after 60 days without activity. As of today, the four related reports the researchers cite have all been closed by the same bot, the most recent yesterday. None got a reply from Anthropic, they say.

106g79v.text: Some WordPress sites can still be attacked while they install the fix for an actively exploited flaw, according to Umut Bayram, the Picus Security researcher who found it. The update that installs the fix still unpacks its files using the site's old, unpatched code, so an attacker who strikes at the right moment can run code on the server. The researcher advises blocking web access to the site's wp-content/upgrade folder before updating. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-119977, affects WordPress 4.7 through 7.1.3. During a core update that uses a complete package, WordPress unpacks a copy of the new version into a temporary folder inside wp-content/upgrade. That copy includes the WordPress installer, and the web server can usually reach it. An attacker with no account who can determine the folder's name and access the installer before WordPress deletes the copy can end up running code on the server. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the flaw to its catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities earlier this week. WordPress released the fix last week in version 7.1.4 and in matching updates for older branches back to 4.7, all listed in its security advisory. The fix gives the temporary folder a random name. But the update that installs the fix unpacks its files using the old code already on the site, as WordPress's updater code shows. On sites running 5.9 or later, that old code names the folder after the downloaded file, so the name can be predicted one last time. Before the fix, an attacker could use the installer to write a new configuration file, wp-config.php, into the temporary copy. The update would then overwrite the site's real file with that file. The part of the fix that stops this already works during the update that installs it, because WordPress copies the files into place using the new code. An attacker who catches the window during that update can still set up the temporary copy of WordPress with their own database, log in to it, and run PHP code with the web server's permissions before the copy is deleted, Bayram says in his technical write-up. From there, the attacker can read or write files in the live WordPress site. Who Is Exposed During the Update Not every update exposes the installer, the researcher says. Complete packages always include the installer files. A smaller partial package, built for one specific starting version, exposes a site only if it happens to contain them. On sites that allow automatic background updates, WordPress installs the fix automatically, via the same updater and the same steps. The Hacker News checked WordPress.org's update service today for several versions. For updates within a branch, such as from 7.1.3 to 7.1.4, it offered a partial package, including for automatic updates. For a move from an older branch, such as from 7.0.7 to 7.1.4, it offered only complete packages. On 4.4 through 5.8, the old code adds random characters to the folder's name. That hides the name unless the site leaks it some other way, such as in an error message, the researcher says. Once 7.1.4 or a branch fix is installed, later updates use a random folder name, and a wp-config.php file in the temporary copy is never copied over the real one. What to Do Before Updating The researcher's first recommendation is to stop the web server from serving wp-content/upgrade at all. WordPress works with that folder directly on disk, so blocking web access does not break updates, he says. Block the folder in the web server configuration. On Nginx, add location ^~ /wp-content/upgrade/ { deny all; }. On Apache, add Require all denied inside a <Directory> block for that folder in the virtual host configuration. If you can only edit .htaccess, add RedirectMatch 403 ^/wp-content/upgrade/ to the .htaccess file in the WordPress root, above the WordPress rewrite rules. Do not put an .htaccess file inside wp-content/upgrade itself. The old updater deletes everything in that folder before it unpacks an update, so the file would be gone when it is needed. Confirm that a request to /wp-content/upgrade/ returns a 403 error. Update to 7.1.4 or to the fixed release for your branch. The other safe route, he says, is a manual update done outside the web root, the folder the web server serves. Back up the site files and database, unpack the new release in a folder the web server does not serve, copy the core files into place without touching wp-config.php or wp-content, and then run the WordPress database update. This way, no temporary installer is ever created in a folder the web can reach. WP-CLI's wp core update command is no substitute, because it runs the same updater and unpacks the package into the same folder. WordPress 4.6 and earlier no longer receive security updates, so there is no fix for them. The researcher says the flaw goes back to WordPress 2.7, released in 2008, and that those sites should move to a supported version. Attacks and What to Check CISA's catalog addition earlier this week was based on evidence of active exploitation, but the agency did not describe the attacks. Wordfence, the WordPress security company that assigned the CVE identifier, saw attack attempts begin nine minutes after it deployed a firewall rule for the flaw on the day of the release. Two of the busiest sources kept checking small groups of sites for about 14.5 hours, which the company says, in its attack analysis, aligns with attempts to catch the moment a site updates. Its score for the flaw in the CVE record is 8.1 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. In its lab tests, the window lasted only seconds. WordPress's own advisory rates the flaw low. Code that its authors describe as an exploit for the flaw has appeared in public GitHub repositories since earlier this week. One of them says its code also works on sites that still use a predictable folder during complete-package updates. Whether the code works has not been established. For sites that stayed on an affected version after the release, Wordfence suggests looking for: unexpected requests to PHP files under wp-content/upgrade administrator accounts no one recognizes plugins no one installed PHP files in wp-content/upgrade that no one put there Update Bayram told The Hacker News on November 6 that whether a partial update is exposed depends on what that specific package contains. A partial package holds only the files that changed between two releases. If those do not include the installer files, the temporary copy cannot run as a WordPress installation, and the installer never becomes reachable. A site also does not always get a partial package when one exists. WordPress falls back to a complete package if the site's core files do not match the official checksums or if the update is a reinstall. The deciding factor, the researcher said, "isn’t partial versus complete. It’s whether the updater already installed on the site has been fixed."

d2s85l.text: A public proof of concept has exposed a flaw in Telegram Desktop that could let attackers steal local files and take over accounts after a user clicks a crafted external link. Tracked as CVE-2026-107181, the vulnerability affects versions before 7.2.9 and carries a CVSS 4.0 severity rating of 8.6 (High). Researcher Beaksec published the technical write-up on October 3, 2026, and updated it on October 7. VulnCheck assigned the CVE that day. The reported attack reaches Telegram’s local session data, making account takeover possible when the victim has not enabled a local passcode. The weakness lies in how Telegram Desktop handles links opened outside the app. When Telegram is already running, another instance passes the link to it through a local communication channel, known as inter-process communication, or IPC. That channel failed to escape a character used to separate records. An attacker could place the character inside a crafted link and make Telegram read part of the link as another command. The CVE record classifies this as CWE-143, improper handling of record delimiters. PoC Released for Telegram Desktop Flaw According to ThreatWire’s research, the injected command could access an outdated internal helper designed for release publishing. The helper could read local files and send them to a chat without permission checks or user confirmation. The result is file theft through Telegram itself. Stolen session files could let an attacker reuse the victim’s logged-in account. Earlier reporting on Telegram account hijacking through voicemail shows another route to account loss, but that method is separate from this Desktop vulnerability. The researcher demonstrated the chain on Windows using Telegram Desktop 6.9.3 and reported that it remained present through 7.2.8. Although the CVE covers Telegram Desktop generally, the write-up does not demonstrate the attack on macOS or Linux. The link must be opened outside Telegram, such as from a browser. Links clicked inside Telegram follow a different processing path and are not affected. A browser may also ask for permission before launching the desktop app. The demonstrated chain depends on automatic group file downloads and settings that allow anyone to add the victim to a group. These conditions matter when judging the “one-click” claim. Previous EvilVideo coverage also highlighted download settings, although that issue affected Telegram for Android rather than Desktop. Telegram fixed the issue in commit db3405699f on September 16 and released version 7.2.9 on September 17. The reported changes remove the legacy helper, escape the record separator, and strengthen handling of mixed record types. The release notes mention only a rendering fix, not the security issue. No vendor security advisory is identified in the supplied reporting. The CVSS 3.1 score is 8.1, while CVSS 4.0 gives 8.6. Both ratings describe the same flaw. Users should update every Telegram Desktop installation to 7.2.9 or later. Until then, restrict group invitations, stop automatic downloads, and enable a local passcode. Treat unexpected browser prompts to open Telegram cautiously. As of October 9, the supplied reporting identifies no known exploitation or CISA KEV listing. A public PoC demonstrates feasibility, not confirmed attacks. The public write-up should not be mistaken for independent attack confirmation. Users who suspect exposure should end other active sessions and review chats for unexpected file uploads. Stops threats before impact with 21 min faster MTTR. 1u9k9io.text: Let’s Encrypt will cut its default TLS certificate lifetime from 90 days to 64 days on February 10, 2027, giving website operators less time between renewals. The change applies to certificates issued or renewed from that date, while subscribers can still choose shorter certificate profiles offering 45 days or roughly six days. Let’s Encrypt Certificate Lifetime According to the October 7 announcement published by Let’s Encrypt, the nonprofit certificate authority confirmed the schedule. Existing certificates will remain valid until their normal expiry dates, and Let’s Encrypt will not revoke them as part of the transition. It expects the final 90-day certificate to expire on May 11, 2027. The shorter lifetime limits how long a certificate can remain trusted after a private key is stolen or a certificate is issued incorrectly. It also makes reliable renewal systems more important, especially for teams still using fixed schedules or manual steps. The move is part of the wider shift toward shorter public TLS certificate lifetimes. Cybersecurity News previously covered the CA/Browser Forum’s plan to reduce maximum validity to 47 days. Let’s Encrypt is moving faster, with its default profile set to 45 days on February 16, 2028, as outlined in its earlier certificate lifetime roadmap. Let’s Encrypt will start issuing 64-day certificates in its staging environment on October 14, 2026. Administrators can use this test service to check renewal behavior before the production change. Staging certificates are not trusted by browsers and should not replace certificates on live websites. For automated setups, the key feature is ACME Renewal Information, or ARI. ACME is the protocol used to request and renew certificates automatically. ARI lets Let’s Encrypt tell a supported client when to renew, helping it adjust to shorter lifetimes without relying on a fixed calendar. Administrators should check their client’s documentation to confirm ARI support. When ARI isn’t available, Let’s Encrypt recommends renewing at about two-thirds of the certificate’s lifetime. For a 64-day certificate, that means around day 43, rather than waiting until the old 60-day renewal point. The authority also recommends searching cron jobs, wrapper scripts, and runbooks for hardcoded values such as 83, 80, or 60. These numbers may reveal renewal rules designed around 90-day certificates. Updating those rules now also prepares systems for the 45-day default planned for 2028. Alongside certificate validity, Let’s Encrypt will reduce authorization reuse from 30 days to 10 days. This is the period during which an earlier domain control check can support another certificate request without repeating that check. The reuse period will fall to seven hours in 2028. Let’s Encrypt says this supports upcoming validation rules and removes the need for separate Certificate Authority Authorization rechecks on older validation data. Most subscribers will not need changes unless their ACME setup specifically depends on authorization reuse. Rate limits will not change because of the shorter lifetimes, according to Let’s Encrypt’s rate limit guidance. ACME endpoints and certificate issuance chains will also remain unchanged. Operators should test the full certificate workflow, including deployment and service reloads, rather than checking renewal alone. Teams managing many websites should also confirm that renewed certificates reach every server and that monitoring checks the certificate actually served to users after each reload. Alerts for failed renewals can help teams catch problems before expiry. The practical priority is dependable automation that keeps certificates current as renewal windows shrink. j5jng0.text: Microsoft is urging organizations to prepare their certificate systems for post-quantum authentication, warning that public key infrastructure (PKI), hardware security modules (HSMs), and security appliances need testing before deployment. Its October 8 guidance says the shift will affect applications, devices, certificate chains, and the processes that keep digital trust working. The message goes beyond protecting encrypted traffic. While many quantum security plans focus on attackers collecting data now to decrypt later, authentication depends on certificates and private keys being issued, stored, checked, renewed, and managed across different vendors. Changing the underlying algorithms can expose gaps across that entire chain. Microsoft Security Researchs noted that organizations often know where TLS protects communications but lack a complete view of certificate dependencies. Their report concerns infrastructure readiness, not a newly discovered malware campaign. Post-Quantum Authentication The main challenge is not simply finding a quantum-resistant algorithm. Businesses must establish whether their existing systems can use new certificates reliably. Older PKI deployments, embedded devices, operational technology, custom applications, and third-party services may contain fixed assumptions that only become visible during testing. Larger post-quantum certificates and certificate chains can affect connection setup, storage, transmission, and network inspection limits. Related work on Cloudflare’s post-quantum certificate authority shows why certificate size and connection speed matter as providers explore different designs for quantum-safe authentication. Those efforts do not remove the need to test enterprise systems individually. HSM providers and security appliance vendors therefore belong in the migration discussion from the start. Teams need to check whether hardware-backed systems support future certificate requirements and whether monitoring, inspection, and certificate-management tools can process the resulting traffic. Support in one application does not establish readiness across the full environment. Microsoft’s PQC TLS Pilot Microsoft launched its Post-Quantum Cryptography TLS Pilot Program on August 27, 2026. It allows approved certificate authorities in good standing with the Microsoft Trusted Root Program to test certificate roots and issuance using ML-DSA-87, a quantum-resistant digital signature algorithm. The focus is compatibility, performance, and day-to-day operations. The August release added seven pilot roots operated by ComSign, DigiCert, HARICA, IdenTrust Services, Sectigo, Shanghai Electronic Certification Authority, and SSL.com. Admissions continue through the end of 2026. Microsoft’s published authentication readiness guidance directs eligible providers to the Trusted Root Program portal for requirements and applications. These certificates are not publicly trusted. Microsoft limits their use to closed environments, custom applications, and enterprise testbeds, explicitly excluding production trust and public-facing websites. Elsewhere, Let’s Encrypt’s certificate roadmap explores Merkle Tree Certificates for public-web authentication, highlighting that separate efforts are addressing different parts of the transition. On supported, correctly configured Windows 11 systems, pilot testing begins with the July 28, 2026 updates. Microsoft names KB5101681, OS Build 28000.2608, for 26H1, and KB5101684, OS Builds 26200.8973 and 26100.8973, for 25H2. ML-DSA certificates can also work with Secure Channel, or Schannel, in supported scenarios. Administrators must confirm platform requirements before testing. Software and hardware readiness should be checked separately. Earlier coverage of Google’s quantum-safe digital signatures described software-based Cloud KMS support with hardware-backed support planned separately. Microsoft similarly urges organizations to ask certificate providers, HSM vendors, software suppliers, and platform vendors about their roadmaps and testing capabilities rather than assume universal support. Security teams should inventory certificate-dependent systems, map public and private trust relationships, and identify equipment with long upgrade cycles. Non-production tests should cover compatibility, performance, and operational workflows. Developments such as OpenSSL’s post-quantum performance improvements offer useful testing context, but preview software and Microsoft’s pilot certificates should not be treated as production-ready replacements. That work should include the full certificate lifecycle, not just a successful connection. Issuance, distribution, validation, renewal, and management all depend on linked systems. Testing those steps together helps teams find process gaps that a standalone algorithm test could miss before they reach live business services. Microsoft recommends a multi-year program with named owners, clear dependencies, and modernization priorities based on test results. Organizations can ask their certificate provider whether it participates in the pilot and offers suitable testing. The practical goal is to uncover failures before quantum-resistant authentication becomes a large-scale deployment requirement. 6tjopr.text: VirusTotal has added daily scanning of the public IPv4 space, giving security teams a new way to find command-and-control (C2) servers and track malware infrastructure. Announced on October 8, 2026, the update records exposed services, port activity, banners, and server fingerprints alongside existing threat intelligence. The change helps researchers look beyond an IP address’s detection score. Earlier reports showed hosting details, passive DNS records, and files that contacted an address. The new data shows what a server exposes now, helping analysts find related hosts that have no malware detections. A new Ports tab lists open, closed, and recently closed ports, together with service names, software versions, and timestamps. Records also include SSH host keys, RDP fingerprints, HTTP headers, and operating system details inferred from service responses. VirusTotal keeps records when ports stop responding. Researchers can therefore check when a suspected C2 service was last seen online and compare that date with changes elsewhere in a campaign. This history adds context that a current detection score cannot provide. VirusTotal Adds Daily Internet Scanning The official announcement describes searches through the web interface and API. Queries such as entity:ip open_port:22 find exposed SSH services. Bracket syntax ties conditions to specific ports, preventing a product on one port from being incorrectly matched with a version on another. These searches build on the methods covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s VirusTotal threat research guide. One investigation started with 91.219.237[.]110, an address listed in APT28 and Havoc collections. Its SSH fingerprint led researchers to 185.146.232[.]3, which had no detections, collections, or communicating files. Both hosts shared an OpenSSH build, nginx configuration, and an unusual certificate name, b4ck.my. Searching that certificate name uncovered a third address, 96.9.125[.]59. Port timestamps suggested one server was being retired around the time another appeared. However, VirusTotal warned that older malware links do not establish current ownership or APT28 attribution because IP addresses can change hands. Fingerprint matches also need careful checks. Some SSH keys appeared across more than 1,400 cloud addresses because server templates reused them. An open port alone is similarly weak evidence. Searching Cobalt Strike’s default team server port returned over 1.5 million addresses, including hosts answering on many ports. Another example exposed a NOX Stealer login panel at 5.175.221[.]206 on port 8443. The host also exposed SMB and RDP, with scan data identifying Windows Server 2022, nginx 1.24.0, and PHP 8.3.33. Combining those traits reduced a search from 4.5 million hosts to ten candidates, not ten confirmed malicious servers. When the panel changed its name to BOMBAY Stealer, browser analysis captured the new title while the exposed services stayed unchanged. Researchers also searched FTP banners containing “conhost,” finding five addresses tied to command-delivery patterns discussed in E4del and PINHOLE research. Port data is available through API records and history endpoints, but not yet through IP Livehunt rules. Saved searches run on a schedule offer a workaround. fow618.text: Alleged internal chats from Silent Ransom Group suggest the criminals collected $206.95 million from 27 firms in roughly six months without encrypting victims’ files. The reported earnings point to the power of data extortion, where attackers steal sensitive records and demand payment to keep them private. However, the payment figures remain unverified, and the group denies breaching its systems or leaking its chats. DataBreaches reported the alleged leak on October 7. The material contains 5,692 messages covering August 27, 2025, through September 29, 2026. Discussions reportedly include victim negotiations, payments, access methods, and members’ spending. An October 8 update said Silent Ransom Group had agreed to an interview but disputed the leak’s origin. Silent Ransomware Extorted Over $200,000,000 The chats mark completed deals as “GOLD.” Adding those entries produces the $206.95 million total. Crystal Intelligence dates the 27 claimed payments between April 3 and September 24, 2026, placing the reported earnings within a period of less than six months. These entries reflect the criminals’ own records, not audited financial results. According to DataBreaches, the median alleged payment was $6 million, while individual amounts ranged from $100,000 to $30 million. White & Case was listed against the largest amount. Nine named firms disclosed breaches relevant to the period. However, those disclosures do not confirm who attacked them or whether they paid the sums shown. Crystal Intelligence’s blockchain analysis found transactions matching the timing of several chat entries. One upstream collection wallet received about 344 bitcoin, valued at roughly $27 million, over six weeks. Researchers could not connect individual victim payments to that wallet. Hence, the evidence supports substantial money movement rather than proving the headline total. Operators trick employees into granting access, steal documents, and threaten to publish them. Law firms have been a major focus because they hold private client information. CybersecurityNews previously covered the group’s IT support impersonation attacks against law firms. Attackers call employees, pose as internal support staff, and persuade them to grant remote access. Legitimate software helps the activity blend into routine work, reducing reliance on malware that security tools might otherwise detect. Related reporting on Luna Moth’s fake helpdesk domains describes websites designed to resemble company support services. Once they gain access, tools such as WinSCP and Rclone can transfer stolen files. The pressure comes from the possible disclosure of confidential records, not a sudden loss of access to business systems. Crystal found instructions to use fresh wallets, keep victim funds separate, and avoid combining payouts. Operators sometimes broke those rules, linking transactions investigators could trace. Smaller payments also reached regulated exchanges, creating potential leads through customer identity records. The analysis describes cash conversion through instant exchangers, couriers, and a Bitcoin-to-Zelle service. For defenders, the attack chain makes identity checks essential. Employees should verify support requests through known internal channels before granting access. Organizations should restrict remote access, deploy phishing-resistant authentication, and train staff to recognize phone-based deception. Working systems don’t prove sensitive files stay safe. 1w6ljoy.text: A malicious Android PDF reader distributed through Google Play has recorded more than 10,000 installs while serving as an installer for the Anatsa banking trojan. The finding shows how a routine document tool can become a route for malware that puts banking passwords and financial accounts at risk. The installation figure describes the reach of the reader app, not a confirmed count of successful banking infections or stolen accounts. The available alert also does not identify affected banks, victim countries, financial losses, or whether Google has since removed this particular listing, wile those details remain unconfirmed. Researchers from Zscaler ThreatLabz identified the malicious installer and shared its indicators in an October 8 alert on X. They described the application as an Android PDF reader with over 10,000 installs and published separate file hashes for the installer and the Anatsa payload, alongside their command-and-control addresses. The discovery follows earlier cases involving similar disguises. In April, a fake document reader campaign used a different package to distribute Anatsa before Google removed that app. That earlier removal should not be confused with the status of the newly reported reader, which the current alert does not establish. Malicious PDF Reader With 10,000+ Installs Anatsa, also known as TeaBot, uses a dropper model: the app installed first acts as a delivery tool for a separate malicious component. This separation helps explain why a download that appears useful can later expose a phone to banking malware. The latest alert identifies both stages but does not provide a full execution trace. In its technical analysis of Anatsa, ThreatLabz documented earlier campaigns that downloaded additional code and presented the final payload as an app update. Some samples checked the device environment before proceeding, helping the malware avoid test systems used by researchers. These are documented family techniques, not confirmed findings for every new sample. ThreatLabz also documented malformed APK archive headers that made older payloads harder to inspect, along with encrypted code loaded at runtime. APK files are Android installation packages; hiding their contents can disrupt tools that inspect files without running them. The new alert does not confirm whether these samples use those methods. The broader use of Google Play stealth loaders shows why unexpected update requests deserve attention even when the original app came from an official store. A request to install an extra component outside the normal update process can move the user from a harmless-looking utility to the banking payload. ThreatLabz has uncovered another new Anatsa installer that is distributed via the Google Play Store. The application is disguised as an Android PDF reader that currently has over 10,000 installs. The IOCs for this campaign are listed below: Google Play Store URL… pic.twitter.com/duQA0myTAi — Zscaler ThreatLabz (@Threatlabz) October 8, 2026 For this campaign, ThreatLabz listed one installer-related command-and-control URL and two payload command-and-control endpoints. Keeping those roles separate matters during an investigation: the installer and the banking trojan are different files, and each has its own published MD5 hash. The alert does not explain the exact contents returned by the installer URL. Why Banking Accounts Are at Risk Earlier ThreatLabz research found that Anatsa requested SMS and accessibility permissions, contacted its control server, and checked for targeted financial apps. The server then supplied fake login pages matching apps on the phone. Credentials entered into those pages were sent to the attackers rather than the bank. A previous Anatsa document reader outbreak reached more than 100,000 downloads and used fake banking screens to capture account details. That history explains the concern around this new reader, but its target list and permission behavior still require sample-specific verification rather than assumptions based on older campaigns. What Android Users Should Do Users who installed the identified reader should remove it, review granted permissions, and scan their phones with a trusted security tool. Keep Google Play Protect enabled and question unexpected requests for SMS or accessibility access. If banking activity looks suspicious, contact the bank promptly and change account passwords from a trusted device. For security teams, the package name can support app inventory checks, while file hashes help match samples against the reported installer and payload. Network logs can be searched for the listed domain and IP endpoints. Matches should be reviewed in context to establish which device communicated, when contact occurred, and whether malware executed. 6er3sq.text: Romania's intelligence agency said it stopped a cyberattack by Russian state-linked hackers on a government institution late last year. The cyberespionage campaign was revealed earlier this week by researchers who found the group targeted Romania in an attempt to intercept emails exchanged with NATO and European Union institutions. The Romanian Intelligence Service (SRI) said Wednesday that it detected the intrusion in December 2025 and took steps to contain the attack and restore the affected systems. The operation was attributed to Turla, a long-running Russian cyberespionage group linked to Moscow's Federal Security Service (FSB). According to the agency, the hackers exploited vulnerabilities in Microsoft systems but Romanian cybersecurity specialists managed to stop the attack. "No exfiltration of sensitive data was identified," the agency said, adding that the affected email service had been restored. The SRI did not identify the targeted government institution or provide details about how the hackers initially gained access. The Slovak cybersecurity firm ESET said Turla used a previously unknown hacking toolkit to compromise government email servers in Romania and Kazakhstan. The malware, dubbed Cereal, allowed attackers to secretly monitor email traffic, collect selected messages and maintain access to compromised Microsoft Exchange servers while avoiding detection. In Romania, the malware was specifically configured to intercept emails sent to or received from NATO and EU institutions, according to ESET. A NATO and EU member bordering Ukraine and Moldova, Romania has repeatedly warned of Russian cyberattacks and other hybrid threats. The country has also reported incidents involving Russian drones entering or approaching its airspace during Moscow's attacks on Ukraine. The SRI said it had informed relevant Romanian authorities about the incident and shared information with European intelligence services and partners within NATO and the EU. Romanian authorities are also investigating other potentially related cyber operations linked to Russia, the agency said. Turla — also known as Secret Blizzard and Venomous Bear — has operated for more than two decades and is considered one of Russia's most established cyberespionage groups. It has previously targeted government agencies, diplomatic missions and defense organizations across Europe, Central Asia and the Middle East. In July, a cyberattack disrupted Romania's national land registry system, taking critical digital services offline in what the agency responsible for the system described as the most serious technical incident in its history. Earlier this year, Romania's then-defense minister warned that government institutions were facing thousands of attempted cyberattacks every day, many of them suspected of originating from Russia. 1i6wy18.text: Suspected Kazakhstan-linked hackers used an artificial intelligence agent to help spy on Central Asian governments, steal sensitive documents and infiltrate critical infrastructure networks, according to new research. Singapore-based cybersecurity firm CloudSEK uncovered the operation after discovering an exposed server belonging to Silent Lynx, a hacking group previously linked to espionage campaigns targeting Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan, Armenia, Belarus and Russia. The server contained more than a dozen gigabytes of data, including stolen government documents, hacking tools and records showing how an attacker used an AI agent to automate parts of the operation. According to the report published Wednesday, the operator relied on Hermes, an open-source AI agent configured to act as an offensive cybersecurity expert. The system primarily used AI models developed by Chinese company DeepSeek. Unlike conventional chatbots, AI agents can execute commands, run software and carry out tasks on behalf of their users. The agent helped with reconnaissance, data collection and erasing traces of activity from compromised systems, researchers said. It was also configured to execute certain potentially destructive commands without requiring additional approval. The operator communicated with the agent in Russian and connected it to a Telegram bot, allowing the hacker to issue instructions remotely from a phone. Government networks compromised One of the group's most significant intrusions targeted Tajikistan, where the hackers maintained extensive access to the national railway network from at least mid-August through early October. After breaking into the network, the attackers gained access to several servers, extracted databases containing login credentials and stole internal documents and operational reports. The hackers also gained access to a much broader collection of government information. Using the credentials of a single railway employee, they logged into Tajikistan's national electronic document management platform, which government ministries and agencies use to exchange official correspondence. The group developed automated tools to download large quantities of files, including thousands of documents sent to or processed by Tajikistan's Defense Ministry in 2026. The stolen material also included correspondence associated with the National Guard, the State Committee for National Security and the State Investment Committee, as well as information about more than 100 government organizations and their employees. CloudSEK also found evidence the group had compromised a server supporting Uzbekistan's Smart Forestry initiative, a government platform used to monitor and manage forest resources. Additionally, the exposed server contained malicious files disguised as official documents from Turkmenistan, including a railway ticket and a regional government report. The files were created and tested in October, suggesting the group was preparing another phishing campaign. Researchers did not establish whether the attacks against Turkmenistan had succeeded. CloudSEK assessed with medium confidence that Silent Lynx has ties to Kazakhstan, citing Russian-language communications and test connections originating from a residential internet provider in the country. Those findings support earlier assessments by cybersecurity researchers that the group is likely based in Kazakhstan, although they do not establish any connection to the Kazakh government. Also tracked as Cavalry Werewolf and YoroTrooper, Silent Lynx has been active since at least 2022 and has previously targeted government agencies, diplomatic organizations and other institutions across Central Asia, Russia and Europe. In October 2025, the group launched a months-long cyberespionage campaign against Russian government agencies and industrial firms, using phishing emails disguised as Kyrgyz government correspondence. 1e307i2.text: Microsoft has confirmed that Windows updates released since the October 2026 Patch Tuesday are causing SQL Server performance and stability issues. As detailed in a Windows release health dashboard update on Wednesday, this is caused by server queries that leave connections open after the queries complete. These connections accumulate instead of closing, degrading server performance over time. "This issue affects SQL Server linked server queries that use OLE DB providers to connect to external databases. Oracle and PostgreSQL connections are among those known to be affected," Microsoft explained. "In affected environments, administrators might observe an increasing number of open connections to external databases, even when the associated SQL Server linked server queries are no longer running." It also added that admins may be able to manually close connections left open due to this bug or restart the SQL service to temporarily address stability and performance issues, but this can also kill active queries and may not fully address the issue, as it will resurface again after some time. Microsoft says the issues impact both client (Windows 10 and Windows 11) and server (Windows Server 2012 and later) systems and will be fixed with an out-of-band Windows update to be released over the next few days. While it works to resolve the bug, Microsoft said IT administrators can reach out to Microsoft Support for Business for a mitigation that can address the issue until a fix is available. In September, Microsoft also shared a temporary workaround for SQL Server crashes on some Windows Server 2025 due to recent memory management changes. The bug affects SQL Server when the Lock Pages in Memory (LPIM) Windows policy is enabled and may cause SQL Server crash dumps, SQL Server services to stop or restart unexpectedly, failures during database maintenance operations, memory corruption errors, and access violation exceptions (with 0xC0000005 error codes). Yesterday, the company also confirmed reports that the November 2026 security updates are failing to deploy on Windows 11 systems where the October preview update has been installed, with affected users seeing 0x80070306, 0x800f0989, or 0x800f0993 error codes. 1q21l6q.text: Apify has rotated critical internal secrets and revoked some third-party OAuth connections after detecting unauthorized access to its internal systems. The incident occurred between November 9 and 10 and was detected the next day at 12:13 UTC. The company reacted by cutting off the attacker's access and launching an investigation to determine the impact. Apify's response involved invalidating internal credentials, rotating API tokens, and resetting all active sessions. Apify is a Czech web scraping and browser automation platform for developers. Businesses use its services to collect data for websites, search results, and social media posts. The platform grew significantly with the generative AI boom, and reports having 80,000 customers, including Microsoft, Samsung, T-Mobile, Accenture, Siemens, the European Commission, and Roche. Rotating customer API tokens and passwords “On 9 and 10 November 2026, an unauthorized third party gained access to parts of Apify’s internal systems,” Apify said in an update on the incident. Apify said it also revoked OAuth connections to external integrations, including GitHub, out of an abundance of caution. Impacted users can expect to be informed via email when it’s safe to reconnect. In one notification, Apify said it had found no indication that account data stored on its platform had been affected by the incident. A sample seen by BleepingComputer informs that impacted customers' Apify API tokens and Apify Proxy passwords have been rotated. In another letter sent to affected customers, the company advises recipients to reset their two-factor authentication (2FA) through the Apify Console, warning that their 2FA codes may have been exposed while assuring them that their passwords remain safe. a4syni.text: Security teams have more alerts, logs, and monitoring tools than ever. Yet when an attack happens, one simple question can still take too long to answer: Who or what is behind this activity, and what can they access? A suspicious login might belong to an employee. An unusual API call could come from a machine account. Or an AI agent might be accessing sensitive systems using permissions nobody has reviewed recently. Your SIEM or EDR may catch the activity. But without knowing who owns that identity, what permissions it has, and which systems it can reach, your SOC is missing a critical part of the story. And that missing context can turn a manageable incident into a much bigger problem. Join this expert-led webinar to learn how real-time identity context can help your SOC investigate threats faster, understand what's at risk, and respond with confidence. The Blind Spot Between Identity and Security Operations Here's the problem. Identity and access management (IAM) teams know who has access to what. Security operations teams monitor suspicious activity and respond to threats. But these teams often work with different tools, different data, and different priorities. When an alert comes in, SOC analysts may know what happened but still struggle to understand what it means. Consider a compromised service account. An analyst might detect suspicious activity, but several questions remain: What applications and systems can this account access? Could an attacker use it to move deeper into the network? How much damage could it cause? Can the account be disabled without breaking a critical business process? These answers matter. Blocking the wrong identity can disrupt production. Waiting too long can give an attacker more room to move. And with machine identities and autonomous AI agents becoming part of everyday operations, the problem is getting more complicated. More Identities, More Access, More Risk Traditional security monitoring was largely built around users, devices, and network activity. Today, organizations also rely on service accounts, API keys, automated workloads, and AI agents that can act without direct human involvement. These identities often have access to important systems and data. If one is compromised, detecting the suspicious action is only the beginning. Security teams also need to understand its permissions, connections, and potential impact. That's where identity context changes the investigation. Instead of treating every alert as an isolated event, analysts can connect suspicious activity to the identity behind it, understand how far an attacker could move, and choose a response that limits damage without unnecessarily interrupting operations. What Does a Better SOC Response Actually Look Like? The goal isn't to add another dashboard or generate more alerts. It's to give analysts the information they need when an incident is unfolding. That means connecting identity intelligence with existing SIEM and EDR alerts, so teams can: Investigate faster: Understand which human, machine, or AI identity is involved. See the real risk: Identify permissions, connected systems, and potential lateral movement. Contain threats safely: Respond to compromised credentials without unnecessarily disrupting critical automation. Work better together: Give IAM and SOC teams shared workflows, clear escalation paths, and common response goals. The difference is simple: knowing that something suspicious happened is useful. Knowing what it can affect and how to stop it is far more valuable. Learn How to Close the Gap In the upcoming webinar, Fuel the SOC with Identity Context: Securing Humans, Machines, and AI Agents, security experts will explore how organizations can bring IAM and security operations together. Drawing on real-world enterprise deployments, the session will cover practical approaches to enriching security alerts with identity context, investigating lateral movement, understanding the potential blast radius of an attack, and improving incident response without disrupting production systems. It will also explain how teams can align around shared metrics, escalation processes, and response playbooks. Your SOC already has the alerts. Now give it the context to act. Register for the free webinar and learn how to turn identity intelligence into faster, smarter security response.

5iil3d.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 12, 2026Vulnerability / Cyber Attack N-able on Thursday said it's investigating a new public disclosure containing claims of additional vulnerabilities in on-premise versions of N-central running version 2026.4.1 HF2. "Based on our initial review, the server issue described depends on a non-default configuration in which the Legacy API is turned on and exposed to the public internet," N-able said in a new advisory. "Legacy API is turned off by default in the product and is not recommended." The company is urging customers to disable Legacy API immediately, if not already. It also noted that hosted environments are not affected by this issue. The incident impacts the following services - N-central On-premise (Americas) N-central On-premise (APAC) N-central On-premise (Europe) The development comes days after N-able released 2026.4.1.26 to address a number of security flaws disclosed by independent security researcher Sean Bales earlier this week. The vulnerabilities are collectively tracked under the name Able2Shell. The new shortcoming, also revealed by Bales, have been codenamed 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell, adding the proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits successfully work against N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26), the update N-able released on November 10, 2026, to resolve Able2Shell. According to the researcher, 4EverAble2Shell enables unauthenticated remote code execution with root privileges on N-central servers. Agent2Shell, on the other hand, leverages more than 10 zero-day vulnerabilities to run commands on managed Windows agents as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, assuming the attacker knows the target appliance ID. Ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, told The Hacker News that targeted N-central probing has been observed against 4EverAble2Shell within hours following the release of the PoC. The activity has originated from the IP address 157.20.241[.]16. There is no evidence of successful exploitation as of writing. In the attack chain observed by the threat intelligence company, threat actors have been observed attempting to achieve initial code execution through a recently disclosed Apache Axis flaw (CVE-2026-90436, CVSS score: 9.8), followed by attempts to escalate privileges to root using 4EverAble2Shell, and then download and execute a shell script from 157.20.241[.]16 using curl. Dewhurst said the development marks the first documented instance of exploitation attempts aimed at CVE-2026-90436, patches for which were released on November 6, 2026. In a post shared on X, watchTowr also said it's seeing probes for 4EverAble2Shell targeting N-Centrals builds with the Legacy API enabled. (This is a developing story. Please check back for more information.)

161ti5y.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 12, 2026Vulnerability / Cloud Security Google Cloud VMs on AMD Turin chips need a guest OS patch and a stop-and-start to protect against three CPU side-channel flaws, Google said this week. The company has already applied mitigations against attacks between VMs, and between VMs and the host. Inside a VM, the flaws may let an attacker with code on the same processor core infer data from other processes or the kernel. The affected machine series are C4D, N4D, H4D, Z4D,, and G4, including bare-metal instances of C4D and Z4D. Turin is the code name for fifth-generation AMD EPYC processors. All three flaws are Transient Scheduler Attacks (TSA). Two of them, TSA-SQ (CVE-2024-36350) and TSA-L1 (CVE-2024-36357), were first disclosed on July 8, 2025, for earlier EPYC processors. AMD now says its Zen 5 processors, which include Turin, are "impacted differently from previously characterized AMD processors." The third flaw, CVE-2026-0004, is new. It may let an attacker who can run code on a system infer data in the processor's L1 data cache. The Xen Project, which maintains the Xen hypervisor, calls the new flaw TSA-Fill. It also says an earlier statement has been corrected: "AMD had previously said that Zen5 CPUs were not vulnerable to TSA-SQ and TSA-L1." Google rates the issue Medium. AMD classifies all three as local attacks with high attack complexity that require only low privileges, according to its Zen 5 bulletin and CVE-2026-0004 advisory. As of today, none of the three is in the KEV catalog of exploited flaws kept by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Neither company reports any exploitation in its bulletins. What Google Cloud Customers Need to Do Google's security bulletin gives these steps for each service: VMs: Install your OS vendor's fix when it ships. Starting this week, the company will update the CPU information that VMs report, so a patched guest kernel can turn on its mitigations. After that update reaches a VM, stop and start it. As the company puts it: "Rebooting the guest OS isn't enough." Bare metal instances: If you run your own OS or hypervisor on a C4D or Z4D bare metal instance, apply your vendor's fixes when they are available. Hypervisors inside a VM: The same CPU information update applies, so patched guest kernels can turn on their mitigations. Stop and start the VM once the update arrives. GKE: Updated node images for Turin-based bare metal instances will be made available, and upgrading nodes picks up the CPU information update. As of today, the bulletin does not yet list them as available. Cloud Run: No action is needed. Customers on older Rome, Milan, and Genoa processors got the same stop-and-start instruction in an earlier bulletin at the time of the original disclosure on July 8, 2025. The company lists nothing to do in the meantime for VMs whose OS vendor has not yet shipped a fix. It also does not say how to tell when the CPU information update has reached a VM. A kernel commit that mitigates TSA on Zen 5, including the new variant, is in the Linux kernel source tree. As of today, Debian has fixed CVE-2026-0004 in its Linux kernel only in its unstable branch. Its security tracker still lists the kernels in bookworm, trixie, and forky as vulnerable. For Turin servers on your own hardware, AMD says both platform firmware and OS updates are needed to mitigate the flaws fully. The mitigation may affect performance, and administrators should weigh the risk to their own workloads, according to its technical guidance. The Xen Project has published hypervisor patches in its Xen advisory. It says microcode for all TSA flaws on Zen 5 has been in linux-firmware since September 23.

1i7jqn6.text: Since mid-August 2026, a phishing operation has been stealing live Google sessions from corporate users. Every check defenders normally lean on to judge a link came back clean, and the operator designed it that way on purpose. The Threat Research team at Material Security spotted the campaign and has since taken down hundreds of attacker domains in an effort the team calls Operation CloudFire. Here’s what the researchers found. The lure: Google Calendar invites The messages show up as Google Calendar invites. Some arrive by BCC, and many come from an organization the recipient has already traded email with. The pretexts are deliberately boring: voicemail notifications, RFP and RFI requests, court summonses, and missed payment notices. Nothing about them stands out in a busy inbox. Most of the links point to Google itself. The usual pattern runs through Google’s own /url redirector, with the real destination tucked into a query parameter. Other waves used share.google and Drive file links the same way, and one variant leaned on Intuit transaction notification links. Whenever a message gets scored, the domain, certificate, and reputation on display are all legitimate. The capture: a reverse proxy in front of Google sign-in Once a victim clicks through, the attacker runs a live reverse proxy in front of the real Google sign-in page. The victim types a password, gets a genuine prompt, and approves it while the operator watches in real time. The server passes each second factor along to Google as it comes in, whether that’s an SMS code, an authenticator code, Google’s Tap-Yes number matching, or phone-based account recovery. None of those controls stop the session from being captured. The framework behind it, known as Nyasher, has been publicly documented since February, after researchers found a hardcoded key in its JavaScript. Why the usual controls stay quiet Reputation systems answer questions about ownership. They ask who registered a domain, what else it has hosted, and whether anyone has complained about it. This campaign was built so every one of those answers came back harmless. It works in three layers. The first is Google’s redirector, which gives the initial hop a trusted Google URL. The second is a Cloudflare Turnstile challenge, and in some builds it’s the real widget served from Cloudflare’s own infrastructure. The third is the password capture page, and that’s where things get tricky for defenders. There’s no static site to scan. JavaScript builds the page in the browser after the visitor clears the challenge, so a crawler has nothing to fetch and a proxy log has nothing to record. As far as the researchers know, nobody had scanned those pages before the campaign was documented. The infrastructure is also meant to be thrown away. Early waves used many lure domains spread across several registrars, and most were registered just days before use. Receiving endpoints went live one to twenty days ahead of the wave they served. One wildcard certificate was issued 46 minutes before the domain it covers was even registered. Blocking any single piece costs the operator a few dollars and an afternoon. What stopping it took Researchers tracked the campaign from the start, following each variant as lures, gates, and endpoints rotated. Once detections were in place, they caught more than 99% of the malicious messages, with a reclassification rate of 0.01%. It’s been steady work, since the attacker kept changing tactics, themes, and lure text to slip past static, machine learning, and agentic detections. What worked was refusing to let any one signal make the call. Reputation alone wouldn’t have caught this. Neither would link analysis, since the first hop is a Google URL and the final page doesn’t exist until a browser builds it. Instead, the detection approach weighs technical indicators alongside the apparent intent of the message, where its links actually end up, and the sending relationship behind it. Any one of those can be enough to act on. A detection built around a single signal inherits that signal’s blind spots, and this operator has put real effort into mapping them. Where the analysis happens matters too. Gateways built to inspect mail in transit aren’t a great fit for calendar invites, and much of this campaign arrives as invites. Calendar invites need to be treated as a threat surface of their own, with the account’s full history used as context next to the technical signals. Where the damage lands A hijacked session leaves its trail in Google Workspace audit logs. A live session reaches mail, Drive, and the ability to grant OAuth access in the victim’s name, so the blast radius goes well past the inbox. That raises a couple of hard questions for security teams. Who’s actually reviewing those audit logs, and how fast can they act on what they find? Could the team revoke sessions, contain OAuth grants, and reset the affected account within an hour? Plenty of programs can’t, and an attacker holding a live session can do a lot in an hour. Operation CloudFire: going after the infrastructure By late September, the researchers decided that tuning rules, retraining models, and updating agents wouldn’t solve this alone. Detection protects customers, but it does nothing about an operator who’s already prepping the next wave. So the team went after the infrastructure. Analysts pulled the gateway and backend URLs as messages were being sent and reported them through Cloudflare’s abuse reporting system. Cloudflare’s abuse team confirmed the fake interstitial and the proxied Google sign-in page behind it, then put its own phishing warning in front of those destinations. That had two effects. First, the attacker’s infrastructure got burned. Every reported gateway and endpoint had to be re-registered, re-pointed, and re-certified before the operator could send again. Second, it protected people well beyond any one company’s customers. Anyone who clicked a reported link saw a warning page instead of a credential form. One month by the numbers These figures only cover organizations that agreed to share data, so the real totals are higher. Over one month of Operation CloudFire, researchers recorded: 68,676 campaign messages blocked 2,112 unique malicious URLs analyzed 897 unique domains taken down 8,570 unique compromised sender addresses across 6,354 root domains The messages also followed a clear rhythm, with sends tracking US business hours. Message delivery by time of day The sender count explains how the campaign earned trust. The attacker controlled each compromised account before the first invite went out, and each one sent invites to the account owner’s saved contacts, among others. Recipients saw a name or domain they knew, on a domain with a clean history, at a sensible time of day. Reputation feeds had no reason to flag any of it. Where things stand now The phishing themes have moved from calendar invites to Google Drive file and document share invites. Researchers haven’t seen a matching jump in other lures or tactics, and activity from this group seems to have scattered. For now, the campaign looks finished. Messages detected by week Domains registered by interval That’s a snapshot, and it could change fast. Rebuilding the infrastructure is cheap, and the framework has been public since February. The operator also shipped an unfinished Microsoft 365 branch alongside the live Google code. It includes a stylesheet path, a second harness, and a title string that decodes to a Microsoft sign-in prompt. None of those paths resolve today, and adding the new brand would only mean dropping in a file, with no code changes. The follow-on is built and waiting. The researchers see the theme rotation as ongoing iteration and expect the next pivot to look a lot like this one, just with a different brand on it. The full technical breakdown, including indicators of compromise and a timeline, is in the companion whitepaper. Teams hunting for this activity in their own environments should start there.

1ngjoh4.text: Microsoft has confirmed reports that the November 2026 security updates are failing to install on Windows 11 systems with the October preview update. This follows widespread reports that the KB5132061 update fails to install, with affected users seeing the installation process lock midway and then trigger 0x800f0989 or 0x800f0993 errors. "When attempting to install the November 2026 Windows security update (the Originating KBs listed above), some devices might be unable to complete the installation. Affected devices might repeatedly attempt to install the update or display error code 0x80070306, 0x800f0989, or 0x800f0993," Microsoft said in a service update seen by BleepingComputer. "This issue affects a limited number of devices that installed the October 2026 non-security preview update (KB5127936). Devices that did not install the October 2026 non-security preview update are not affected." Microsoft also told IT administrators that the installation issues will resolve automatically for all affected customers by Friday morning and that end users do not need to take any action to receive the fix. "All affected devices should be repaired in 24 to 48 hours starting from November 11, 2026, 10am PT. Once your device receives the repair, it will automatically download and install the November 2026 security update via Windows Update," it added. The company also urged admins still receiving reports of installation issues after 48 hours to contact Microsoft Support. This is not the first time Microsoft has had to address Windows update installation issues since the start of the year. In March, it had to pull a buggy Windows 11 non-security preview update (KB5079391) because of 0x80073712 errors during installation. In May, it also fixed installation failures and 0x800f0922 errors when deploying the May 2026 Windows 11 security update (KB5089549). More recently, in June, Microsoft warned users that they may encounter issues installing the latest monthly updates and see 0x80073712 or 0x800f0993 errors on some Windows devices upgraded to Windows 11 24H2 or 25H2. 2r1wo4.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 12, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security PTC has released patches for a new critical vulnerability impacting Windchill and FlexPLM software that, if successfully exploited, could result in remote code execution. The security flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-126325, carries a CVSS v4 score of 9.2 out of a maximum of 10.0. It has been described as a case of improper input validation and deserialization of untrusted data that could result in remote code execution via crafted requests. "A critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability has been reported in PTC Windchill and PTC FlexPLM," according to a description of the flaw on CVE.org. "The vulnerability may be exploited through the deserialization of untrusted data." The CVE record lists the following versions as affected - PTC Windchill: 11.0 M030, 11.1 M020, 11.2.1.0, 12.0.2.0, 12.1.2.0, 13.0.2.0, 13.1.0.0, 13.1.1.0, 13.1.2.0, 13.1.3.0, 13.1.4.0 PTC FlexPLM: 11.0 M030, 11.1 M020, 11.2.1.0, 12.0.2.0, 12.1.2.0, 13.0.2.0, 13.1.0.0, 13.1.1.0, 13.1.2.0, 13.1.3.0 "If your Windchill or FlexPLM environment is hosted by PTC, the patches have been applied on their behalf. No action is required on your part," PTC said in a statement posted on its website. "If your Windchill or FlexPLM environment is not hosted by PTC, we urge you to apply the patch as soon as possible to help protect your systems." The disclosure comes nearly five months after another critical remote code execution (RCE) issue in Windchill and FlexPLM (CVE-2026-12569, CVSS score: 9.3) came under active exploitation. Then, in July 2026, it emerged that threat actors linked to the Cl0p ransomware operation were weaponizing the flaw as part of a data extortion campaign designed to drop JSP web shells and exfiltrate sensitive product data from manufacturing companies and industrial enterprises. "PTC software is a textbook target for initial access brokers and ransomware operators and a significant enabler of triple extortion campaigns," Yordan Ganchev, principal threat intelligence specialist at watchTowr, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News. "It allows malicious actors to reach far and wide within victim networks, encrypt and exfiltrate proprietary data, and disrupt industrial processes. In many cases, the impact across these environments has downstream implications for time-sensitive manufacturing, logistics, and fulfillment processes, resulting in material costs per hour of downtime." Organizations running PTC Windchill and FlexPLM products are recommended to patch exposed systems as soon as possible and monitor for signs of code execution, backdoor access, or web shells on the host. If patching is not an immediate option, it's essential to apply network restrictions to limit the risk of compromise.

120cxv3.text: Multiple threat actors are abusing GSocket, a legitimate open-source remote access tool, to maintain access to Linux servers even after patching the vulnerabilities exploited to gain initial access. Since March, detections of malicious GSocket activity have increased, particularly in attacks targeting web applications and hosting environments. GSocket allows attackers to reach systems behind firewalls or NAT by intercepting network connections and replacing the program's conventional IP-layer communication with its own transport layer, which routes traffic through the Global Socket Relay Network. Since both endpoints initiate outbound connections to the relay, which matches them and brokers an end-to-end encrypted session, an attacker can reconnect without needing the compromised server's IP address or hostname. This makes it more difficult for defenders to disrupt attacks using IP- or domain-based access control lists. According to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry, GSocket-related detections increased by 356.2% between March and August. Microsoft explains that both the compromised server and the attacker connect outbound, hence the server needs no inbound listener implants, making the attack stealthier. Communication scheme Source: Microsoft “The compromised host and the operator both connect outbound to the relay, which bridges the two sessions,” Microsoft explains. “The host needs no inbound listener or public IP address, and network address translation does not prevent the connection.” The same model also removes the need for attackers to use a dedicated command-and-control (C2) server. Microsoft says inbound firewall rules don’t catch the malicious traffic, although egress filtering and outbound monitoring can. Of the detected incidents, 87.1% related to web applications and hosting. PHP web apps and cPanel hosting accounted for 63.9%, and Apache accounted for 24.3%. The researchers observed attackers disguising GSocket as kernel threads and using cron jobs, systemd services, and shell startup files for persistence purposes. In some cases, the attackers attempted to exploit the “Dirty Frag” Linux kernel flaw (CVE-2026-43284) to gain root privileges on the host. General attack chain Source: Microsoft Microsoft says most targets of GSocket activity are in the education and research sector, followed by technology and communications, manufacturing, and government entities. The researchers recommend that system administrators remove GSocket and associated files from potentially impacted servers, and verify that outbound connections to its relay network have stopped. They also advise restricting outbound traffic to predetermined destinations and auditing cron jobs, systemd services, and shell startup files for rogue additions. Generally, keeping the OS and applications up to date, including patching for CVE-2026-43284, is a strong measure against this and other attacks.
