1sk6nlb.text: A critical flaw in MongoDB Server allows an unauthenticated attacker to send two requests that trigger a crash on the database server. The crash occurs only if that server is later chosen to take over as the main server while it still lacks some recent changes. MongoDB, the company that makes the database, released fixed versions earlier this week. The affected servers are members of a replica set, a group of MongoDB servers that keep copies of the same data. One member, the primary, serves as the main server and handles all new writes, while the others replicate them. If the primary becomes unavailable, the other members hold an election to pick a new primary. Researchers at Datadog Security Labs reproduced the crash in a lab and published their findings yesterday. On vulnerable versions, turning on authentication does not stop the two requests. An attacker cannot make the targeted member fall behind or win an election, or see when either happens, the researchers said. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-118383, is a use-after-free: the server ends up using memory it has already freed. MongoDB rated it 9.5 out of 10 on the CVSS 4.0 severity scale. The company said it found the flaw itself and was "not aware of any attempts to take advantage of this vulnerability." Affected members include the shard and config server members of sharded clusters. A standalone mongod, a single server outside any replica set, is not affected. Each affected branch has a fixed release, listed below and in the CVE record. Every earlier version in a branch is affected, back to the branch's first release. MongoDB Atlas clusters automatically receive fixed versions during maintenance, the company said in its security announcement. Customers who defer maintenance should apply the upgrade as soon as possible. Self-managed deployments need the fixed release on every replica set member. After upgrading, check the version each member is running, including members in containers and any that were offline during maintenance. The 8.2 branch is not among the affected versions listed, and its newest release is 8.2.12. But a proof of concept published on GitHub reports that 8.2.12 still exhibited the bug in a lab test using a test-only setting. The 8.2 branch reached end of life on July 31, according to the company's lifecycle schedule. Past that date, a version no longer receives fixes, including security fixes. Until a member can be upgraded, the researchers advise restricting network access to the database to only the systems that need it. That limits who can send the two requests but does not fix the flaw. A member who wins an election first catches up by applying the writes it missed before it accepts new ones. The flaw is in the cleanup that runs when this catch-up step ends, according to the Datadog researchers' technical analysis. The two requests are ping commands that carry a readConcern.afterOpTime value. Each asks the server to wait until replication reaches a certain point, and the server records a pending notification for it, called a waiter. Planting the waiters does not crash the server. They do not expire, and stay in place until the member restarts, rolls back or steps down from primary. The crash needs the member who received the requests to win a later election, even though it is behind another member. When catch-up ends, the cleanup runs twice, reusing memory that was already freed, and the new primary crashes before it accepts any writes. Once those conditions are met, the crash does not depend on winning a timing race, the researchers said. In the lab, the researchers caused the member to fall behind and forced a failover themselves by using admin access to pause and stop mongod processes. Only the two requests came from a client without credentials, and that client could not write to the database. On version 8.0.34, the member crashed with a segmentation fault, leaving the lab cluster without a primary. Another deployment might elect a new primary and keep running. In the fixed version 8.0.37, the server rejected both requests as unauthorized at once, and the member kept running. One part of the fix lets only system users use readConcern.afterOpTime. MongoDB says the flaw may also result in arbitrary code execution in the server process under certain conditions. In the lab, though, "we did not achieve code execution," the researchers said. Their results also do not show how often the attack would work in other setups. The proof-of-concept code reproduces the bug in a lab replica set, according to its author. Its reliable mode requires a test-only setting that a remote attacker cannot enable. Its stated impact is a crash or memory corruption, with no claim of code execution. The second part of the fix stops the cleanup from running twice even when waiters are already in place, the researchers said. They did not test that part themselves. In the proof-of-concept lab test, which ran with authentication turned off, the fixed 8.0.37 accepted the planted waiters but ran the cleanup only once. To look for planting or a crash, check the server's structured logs for these signs from the researchers' vulnerable run: Log event: a COMMAND "Slow query" entry (ID 51803) for an unauthenticated ping carrying readConcern.afterOpTime that ended with MaxTimeMSExpired. Log event: a member entering primary catch-up (ID 21359), then exiting it twice (ID 21363) in one transition. Log event: a fatal signal or backtrace involving CatchupState::abort_inlock() after those exits. A normal election or a single catch-up exit does not point to this flaw. The requests may also arrive before the failover, so check earlier logs from the same member too. Whether the request fields are logged depends on logging settings, and the attr.remote field may show a loopback address instead of the client's real IP.

1uuxot7.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 12, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security A flaw fixed in Node.js this week lets unauthenticated clients crash servers that use the runtime's built-in HTTP/2 support on the 24.x and 26.x release lines. A second HTTP/2 flaw can cause a server to send a client pieces of its memory, including responses intended for other connections. Fixed versions were released for all three supported lines: 22.23.5, 24.22.3, and 26.13.1. The crash flaw, CVE-2026-123863, needs only a default HTTP/2 server that replies before the request body has fully arrived. The Node.js project calls that behavior typical. The crash works over both TLS and cleartext connections. The memory flaw, CVE-2026-123866, affects all three lines. From 24.22.0 and 26.9.0 onward, a client alone can trigger it. On 22.x and older 24.x and 26.x builds, it can still be triggered when the server itself closes a stream partway through a response, for example after an idle timeout. A separate flaw in Node.js HTTPS servers, CVE-2026-123864, can allow an unauthenticated client to read memory from other connections, "including TLS private keys and other users' requests," the project says. It affects all three supported lines. The flaw needs a handler that calls res.flushHeaders() before the request body has fully arrived and later calls res.end() with data. Reading the leaked memory also needs a route that sends back or stores a request body. Plain HTTP servers built with node:http are not affected. The release fixes 16 vulnerabilities in Node.js itself, seven of them rated high. The other four high-rated flaws, and the servers they affect, are: CVE-2026-123865: a client can make any default HTTP/2 server hold memory and file descriptors permanently, on all three lines. CVE-2026-123874: a client can corrupt server memory on 24.x and 26.x when the server serves files with stream.respondWithFile() or stream.respondWithFD(). On all three lines, canceling such downloads can also crash the server (CVE-2026-123875, rated medium). CVE-2026-126051: a client can crash a TLS server on 24.x and 26.x if the server uses the SNICallback, OCSPRequest, newSession or resumeSession hooks, or server.addContext(). CVE-2026-123872: on a TLS server with stricter client-certificate rules for some hostnames, a client approved for another hostname can switch to a stricter one during TLS 1.2 renegotiation without meeting its rules. All three lines are affected. The eight flaws above are all in Node.js's own HTTP/2, HTTPS and TLS server code, so they matter where a Node.js process accepts those connections itself. Updating to the fixed version for each line is the only fix in the project's security advisory. It lists no workaround for servers that cannot update yet. End-of-life lines, including 20.x and 25.x, get no fix in this release, and the project says such versions are always affected. The advisory does not report any attacks using the flaws. It also does not say whether servers that met the conditions for the HTTPS flaw should replace their TLS keys or other secrets after updating. Five of the flaws, including CVE-2026-123863 and CVE-2026-123864, were reported by Chris Rohlf in collaboration with Claude and Anthropic Research, according to the advisory.

r1dllr.text: Starting Tuesday, an attacker used stolen credentials for 4,837 GitHub accounts to plant a secret stealer in repositories those accounts could write to, according to Aikido Security, a security software company. The stealer is built to take the secrets and cloud credentials that a repository's CI workflows can reach. It ran in at least 1,806 repositories, where the attacker has likely collected those credentials, the company says. Each attack started with a pull request titled docs: dependency audit notes, opened from a branch named wfx-docs to test whether the account could write to the repository. These test pull requests were opened in 61,764 repositories, and the stealer followed in some of them. In a separate analysis, researchers at SafeDep, which sells software supply chain security tools, counted 8,093 repositories that received malicious commits between 12:46 UTC on Tuesday and 04:36 UTC today. That count covers every repository that received malicious commits, not only those where the stealer ran. Their search covered only the default branches of public repositories, so the true total is higher, the researchers say. In 7,309 of those repositories, the stealer was added to an existing workflow. In 771, it came as an npm postinstall hook, which also runs on a developer's machine during npm install. After pushing the stealer, the attacker usually reverted the change within minutes. Where the stealer ran, its logs were deleted, usually along with the run itself. In those repositories, every secret and cloud role available to the workflows should be treated as compromised. More pull requests with the same title were opened early today, after the company's own GitHub search ended on Wednesday, a check by The Hacker News found. Three that were checked, opened between 05:04 and 05:38 UTC, came from wfx-docs branches. It is not clear whether the stealer followed. Any account that opened one of the attacker's test pull requests is compromised, even if the stealer never ran, Aikido said in its technical analysis. The analysis does not explain how the attacker obtained the credentials. SafeDep's researchers advise owners of affected repositories to revoke the commit author's tokens, OAuth app grants, SSH keys, and sessions, and to turn on 2FA. Owners should also rotate every secret and variable the repository can read. Anyone who ran npm install on an affected commit should treat that machine as compromised and rotate its keys. In most other repositories that received a test, nothing was pushed afterward, or the stealer did not run due to the repository's settings or the account's permissions. The figures cover only the public repositories the company could see. The tests also reached repositories that the compromised accounts did not own. Of the test pull requests, 10,431 were submitted via collaborator or organization access, and 92% of those were still open when the company checked. Signs a Repository Was Hit Check for these signs, from Tuesday onward, in any repository you can write to: Branch: wfx-docs Branch: chore/[a-z0-9]{8}, short-lived Branch: ci-check-[0-9]{4} Pull request title: docs: dependency audit notes Commit message: ci: refresh build cache, which adds about 1,500 lines to an existing workflow Commit message: chore: add ci helper, which adds a .ci-xxxxxx.sh script and a postinstall hook in package.json that runs it on any npm install Commit message: chore: add dependency audit workflow, which adds .github/workflows/build-audit-xxxxxx.yml on a chore/ branch Commit message: chore: initial commit, pushed before a new workflow file in an empty repository Commit message: ci: restore Commit message: ci: cleanup SHA-256 (stealer script): 89695abb392d5cfd4972672961e644bb46baa98aa1ed7173c2a2816c762735cf IP: 194.150.166[.]244:8080/exfil IP: 18.143.168[.]96:8080/exfil IP: 153.75.82[.]159:8080 A repository can show no wfx-loot artifacts, wfx- cache entries, or WFX-BEGIN step summaries and still have lost data. A missing run number on the attacker's commit is the more reliable sign that the stealer ran. The stealer sends data by HTTP POST to the addresses above or to a Telegram chat, the SafeDep researchers found. In a sample of 200 payload commits, about a fifth used Telegram only. The stealer is built to collect credentials from every source on the runner, according to the company. They include GitHub Actions secrets and variables, the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN, OIDC and Actions runtime tokens, keys for AI services, and secrets in the memory of the runner's own processes. It reads credential files for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, PyPI, SSH, and other tools from their usual locations. It also copies the repository, its last 100 commits, and recent workflow artifacts. On self-hosted runners, it takes cloud credentials from instance metadata as well as Docker container state and systemd units. The stealer also has settings for private repositories, and the company says that suggests it may be running in them. The stealer is designed to use those credentials to reach deeper into cloud accounts. It exchanges GitHub OIDC tokens for AWS, GCP, and Azure sessions, and on AWS it can create long-lived access keys for IAM users. Some of its steps are built to survive credential rotation. It can rewrite an AWS role's trust policy to open the role to any AWS account. It can also add federated identity credentials with the prefix wfx-ci- to Azure AD applications. Workflows in the compromised repository can then sign in to Azure without a stored secret, even after all tokens are rotated. To find these backdoors, the researchers suggest checking for: Entra ID: federated credentials named wfx-ci-* that you did not create AWS CloudTrail: AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity or AssumeRole sessions named wfx-*, followed by CreateAccessKey or UpdateAssumeRolePolicy GCP: GenerateAccessToken and SignJwt calls from your GitHub workload identity pool Vault: JWT logins from the GitHub OIDC issuer The stealer reached at least one Packagist package and one Go module through automated publishing triggers. At least 50 of the compromised users appear to publish packages for npm, Go, Packagist, PyPI, or crates. The attacker appears to be after CI secrets rather than trying to spread through packages, the company says. Version 3.14.3 of the Packagist package digitalelvis/neuronai-studio is malicious, and the company advises treating any machine that installed or opened it as compromised. Its package listing shows the version was published on Wednesday. Early today, the version was still listed, under a notice that versions of the package had been flagged as malware. A normal composer install does not run the stealer, but running npm install inside the package's vendor directory does, the researchers found. Users should block v3.14.3 and pin v3.14.2 or earlier. Two versions of the Go module github.com/onuragtas/docker-env, v1.0.278 and v1.0.280, carry the stealer only in a GitHub Actions workflow file. The Go code and release binaries are unchanged, and Go builds never run workflow files, so users of the module may not have been affected. The company still recommends removing those versions. The researchers also found the stealer in another Go module, github.com/vkuznet/gocurl, in pseudo-version v0.0.0-20261111095532-8d5aad0cb0da, inside a workflow that has never run. Users should block that pseudo-version. The stealer also reached 28 WebdriverIO repositories through commits authored as the bot account wdio-bot. No package release was affected, but the bot's token should be treated as stolen. The company found that the accounts used this week overlap with those hit in GhostAction's October wave, in which stolen GitHub accounts pushed secret-stealing workflows into repositories. Accounts hit in October were about 1,000 times more likely than other active accounts to be used this week. In more than 100 repositories, the new stealer was added to October's workflow files, leaving the older step that sends data out in place. Aikido said, "we don't attribute November to the same actor at this stage," because the infrastructure, tools, and methods differ, and stolen credentials often end up with several attackers.
